#7586. New Brennan Center Report on Curbing Executive Power

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Many of their recommendations are well-taken.

The NYU Brennan Center for Justice recently published a valuable report entitled "Seven Solutions to Rein In Abuses of Executive Power." The Brennan Center is well to the left of me. But I agree with the vast majority of their recommendations here. We do indeed have an overgrown executive, and it needs to be pared back. I particularly agree with the excellent section on constraining emergency powers:

With just a signature, presidents can declare a national emergency and unlock special powers contained in more than 130 statutory provisions. These run the gamut from the seemingly trivial to the near-dictatorial, including powers to shut down or take over communications infrastructure, freeze Americans' bank accounts, and control domestic transportation. They are intended for sudden, fast-moving crises that Congress can't address quickly or flexibly enough. But presidents of both parties have stretched the meaning of "emergency" far beyond reason, enabling them to draw from a growing stockpile of statutory authorities with few real safeguards.

There are currently 51 active states of emergency, and the longest-running has lasted 47 years.10 Any emergency that persists for generations is, by definition, not an emergency; it's a problem that can be addressed through ordinary lawmaking. Yet presidents have used emergency powers to bypass Congress and unilaterally advance their policy goals.11

The National Emergencies Act once allowed Congress to terminate emergencies with a simple majority vote and without the president's signature. But the Supreme Court struck down that procedure, known as a legislative veto, in 1983. Today, ending an emergency effectively requires a two-thirds majority in both chambers to override a presidential veto.

Congress should amend the National Emergencies Act to constrain executive overreach.12 Emergency declarations should expire automatically after 30 days unless Congress approves a one-year extension, renewable annually with Congress's assent. And presidents should be required to share detailed reports on their uses of emergency powers. Proposals along these lines have received widespread bipartisan support, with versions of these reforms overwhelmingly passing out of the relevant House and Senate committees in 2024.13

Additionally, Congress should amend specific emergency statutes whose extensive delegations of power and inadequate safeguards make them susceptible to misuse. Of particular concern is the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, the most frequently invoked presidential emergency authority.14 Sanctions imposed under this law can equate to a "financial death sentence" lasting years or decades.15 Although the Supreme Court blocked Trump's effort to use the law to set global tariffs, the potential for other abuses remains.

I completely agree, and have previously advocated similar reforms, myself. Brennan is right that IEEPA should be tightened up. While the Supreme Court did rule (in a case I helped litigate) that IEEPA cannot be used to impose tariffs, it still includes a lot of other dangerous powers.

I would add, as I did in this article, that invocations of emergency powers should be subject to  nondeferential judicial review, to ensure that they are used only in the event of genuine emergencies, not bogus ones. Congress would do well to amend relevant emergency statutes to make clear that such nondeferential judicial review is available.

I also strongly endorse Brennan's recommendations on constraining laws governing the domestic use of the military. The Supreme Court did strike down Trump's attempts to use bogus pretexts for federalizing the National Guard; the Ninth Circuit recently reinforced that ruling by rejecting the administration's broad definition of what qualifies as a "rebellion" justifying federalization. But, as the Brennan report indicates, there is still a lot of potential for abuse, especially when it comes to the Insurrection Act.

I also agree with the Brennan report's advocacy of constitutional amendments eliminating presidential immunity from criminal liability for acts undertaken in office, and barring him from pardoning crimes committed by" members of their inner circle, including immediate family members and senior administration officials" and those "convicted of crimes ordered by the president or committed on the president's behalf."

I doubt that these amendments have much chance of being enacted, given the extreme difficulty of passing any constitutional amendment. On the other hand, the reforms to emergency powers and domestic use of the military can be adopted through ordinary legislation. In some cases, they can also be bolstered by stronger judicial review under existing laws and provisions of the Constitution.

I do have a few disagreements with the report. For example, it is not clear to me that the Supreme Court's decision in Trump v. Slaughter goes as far as the authors suggest. The decision's scope remains uncertain. Among other things, it's not clear how wide a range of federal agencies it applies to and how to reconcile it with Trump v. Cook, decided on the same day. I also think they may overestimate Slaughter's impact, since most federal agencies are already not independent in the sense that there are legal constraints on the presidents' power to fire their heads.

I would also have liked to see more recognition that curbing excessive executive power requires curbing the scope of federal power generally. It is virtually impossible to have a federal government that regulates almost every aspect of human activity without simultaneously delegating vast - and often dangerous - discretion to the executive.

That said, the vast majority of the Brennan report's recommendations are well-taken. I hope future Democratic administrations and members of Congress act on them.

For those keeping score, it's worth noting that Brennan Center emergency powers expert Elizabeth Goitein, one of the authors of the report, is a long-time critic of abuses of emergency powers under Democratic administrations, as well as Republican ones. For example, she condemned President Biden's attempt to use emergency powers to effectuate massive student loan forgiveness. And so did I.

#7584. If You Spot OTR on a Truck, Here’s What It Means

Those three letters on a semi-truck usually refer to long-distance driving. Learn what OTR means and how different trucking routes work.

Trucks are full of weird and useful features that most people overlook without knowing their real purpose. Some have long spikes on their wheels. Others might feature amber lights on top. You might even see diamond shaped signs. But what about OTR written on a truck?

What can look like a government code can have a specific meaning in the trucking industry. Learn what OTR means, how long-haul work compares with shorter routes, and why the context matters.

In trucking, OTR stands for “over-the-road.” It refers to long-haul trucking, where drivers transport freight across long distances, often through several states or into Canada. According to trucking company Schneider, OTR drivers can spend weeks away from home. Many drive trucks with sleeper cabs that provide a place to rest between shifts.

OTR describes the type of work, not a specific truck. It’s also not a required marking. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA) requires certain identifying information, including a company’s name and USDOT number, on interstate commercial trucks, but OTR isn’t part of that requirement.

The letters can also mean something different depending on where they appear. In the tire industry, OTR stands for “off-the-road,” referring to heavy-duty tires used on construction and mining equipment. OTR Diagnostics is also the name of a maintenance tool that helps truck owners check engine problems and other vehicle information.

OTR truck drivers transport freight over long distances, often making several stops along the way. Their jobs can also involve inspecting their trucks, handling delivery paperwork, and sometimes helping load or unload cargo.

Because these trips can last for weeks, drivers often sleep in their trucks or stop at other places along their routes. The FMCSA limits how long commercial drivers can drive without taking required breaks and rest periods.

Drivers who operate most full-size tractor-trailers need a Class A commercial driver’s license (CDL). Depending on the company and route, drivers may spend several weeks working before returning home.

OTR drivers cover the longest distances and may spend weeks away from home. Regional drivers work within a particular area of the country, often returning home weekly or more frequently. Local drivers generally stay closer to home and return after each shift, although they can still work long hours.

There’s also dedicated trucking, where drivers regularly transport freight for the same customer or between the same locations. These routes can be local, regional, or long-distance, depending on the company.

The exact distances and schedules vary between employers, so the terms don’t always describe the same mileage or amount of time away from home.

When the weather turns chilly, most people pull out heavy coats, rugged boots, and, of course, ice melts. Ice-melting products are an important line of defense against slick, dangerous conditions on driveways, sidewalks, and other surfaces. Without using them, drip lines and low spots can turn into serious home safety hazards.

We researched and tested 10 different ice melt products to see which delivered the best results. Nearly every brand improved walking conditions and had a positive impact on overall traction and safety. Some were more capable of handling the heavy-duty demands of high-traffic residential and commercial areas. Others were safer for pets and the environment, making them great for home use. Since it’s common practice to apply ice melts to areas where pets and kids may walk or play, we also spoke with the medical director of a veterinary emergency group to get their insights.

While they may not be quite as diverse as snowflakes, ice melts do come in a variety of forms, each with its own distinct features. We tested each product in the following list ourselves to help you choose the best ice melts for your needs.

This Natural Rapport ice melt is one of the safest ice melts for pets, plants, and the environment. It’s less corrosive on metal, wood, and concrete than conventional rock salt, and it is also safer on carpet and other flooring materials, should your furry friends or kids track it into the house.

Many environmentally friendly products melt slowly because they use mild formulas. But we were pleasantly surprised by how fast-acting and long-lasting this ice melt was. Its time-released formula not only started working right away but also kept melting, preventing our sidewalks and driveway from refreezing. The crystals are green, so it was easy to see where we’d applied them, helping to prevent waste. Also, our dogs repeatedly walked over the colorful ice melt with no adverse reactions.

Ultimately, this ice melt took the top award because it offers a combination of performance and environmental friendliness. Snow Joe is a leader in snow removal products, and it has formulated a fantastic ice melt product with the Premium Enviro Blend Ice Melter. It’s made for extreme cold and has a chemical composition designed with the environment, pets, and people in mind.

This blend has an anti-corrosion agent that helps it break down easily while minimizing damage to concrete, asphalt, and yards. It also has a green dye that makes monitoring its performance and presence on the ground easy. When the green coloring fades, it’s time to add more. This formulation did an excellent job melting ice and maintaining clear walkways. We also had a property management company test it, and they were impressed.

Though some may prefer ice melt that comes in a bucket or ice melt shaker, we found the durable bag-style packaging of this Snow Joe eco-friendly ice melt easy to reach into and move around. Be aware, however, that if the open bag gets wet, the contents will bind together and consolidate into a giant rock. We kept ours in the garage, and it was fine.

Since almost all ice melt formulations contain salt or chlorides, this salt-free option from Safe Paw is quite unique. It’s a great choice if your household is sensitive to salts or if using anything corrosive is not viable (such as around a classic car, near expensive equipment, or on a newly paved surface). It’s also nonconductive, making it safe around electrical components.

This product comes in a granular form and doesn’t have sharp edges like rock salt. Thanks to its nonabrasive texture, our dogs had zero issues walking through it. They even played right where we tested this product and showed no adverse effects. That’s also likely partly due to the blend’s chemical composition, which isn’t as aggressive as other formulas. When people think about removing snow from roofs, they often imagine doing so manually. That’s because few ice melt products are made to address ice buildup on roofs—which is what makes this ice melt such a unique product. The tablets are composed of calcium chloride and designed to be thrown onto roofs to prevent snow and ice buildup from wreaking havoc on gutters and adding weight to vulnerable areas. For those living in areas with heavy snowfall where ice dams often form, they are a worthy investment.

During testing, we aimed for problem spots and tossed the tablets up. Still, for their intended purpose, they worked well.

The Roof Melt tablets aren’t granular or spreadable, so they aren’t compatible with larger surface areas like driveways. You could probably use them on the ground where drainage is constricted and problematic, but other options will be more economical for that purpose. If you deal with dangerous ice dams on your roof, however, these tablets are worth having around to quickly and easily resolve the issue.

The best way to determine how effectively various ice melts perform is to fully test each product. As residents of Montana, we began our testing in the aftermath of a winter snowstorm that turned bitter cold. We applied the products to gravel, pavement, and grass in temperatures as low as -6 degrees Fahrenheit.

As the snow went through several melt/freeze cycles over the coming days, it formed icy spots under our rooflines and in several low spots. We tested the ice melts in freezing temperatures on water drips and overnight freezes that created walking hazards each morning. We analyzed how long it took to apply each product, how quickly they melted ice and snow, their degree of pet friendliness when used around our dogs, and a number of other hands-on factors. Lastly, we compared pricing, packaging, and ease of application.

Ice melt products are designed for use either before or after snow or ice has fallen. Their application prevents ice from forming or melts it into a slush that’s easier to clear with a standard snow shovel. Each type of ice melt will perform differently depending on its form and chemical composition. Other variables, such as temperature, ground type, melting time, and environmental impact are essential to consider before purchasing an ice melt product.

Ice melt is available in solid and liquid formulations, each with pros and cons. Solid ice melt typically comes in pellets and granules. It works well for many applications and is typically the go-to solution for road crews dealing with icy and snowy weather. Pellets and granules are generally less expensive and easier to store than liquid formulas, and they add a “crunchy” texture on surfaces that adds grip for walking and driving. Their main downsides are that they scatter more easily across icy surfaces, making them harder to apply with precision, and that they tend to be slower acting and more likely to clump together, which sometimes makes them less effective.

Liquid ice melt is a wise choice for lower-temperature situations and times when faster results are necessary. That said, some products must be applied before ice forms rather than after. When applied, liquid is less likely to scatter, staying in place for longer-lasting results. Liquid de-icers, which tend to cost more, can be more challenging to transport and store because of their weight. Plus, if heavy rain ensues, the product can get washed away.

Self-heating ice melt, which comes in pellet and granular form, generates its own heat when in contact with ice and snow—a process known as an exothermic reaction. Unlike other products that must absorb moisture to create a brine to melt the ice, self-heating ice melt can get right to work.

Ice melts work by absorbing the moisture on the top of the ice, creating what’s called brine, and working its way down to break the bond between the ice and the surface. This creates cracks and flakes that are safer to walk on and easier to remove. All of these products have a temperature limit. If temperatures plummet beyond a product’s ice melting point, the chemicals will no longer be effective. Here’s what to expect from the various ice melt types available:

Many of the chemicals in ice melts can potentially damage surfaces, so it’s important to consider where the product will be used. The most common areas—driveways, sidewalks, decks, and porches—can be composed of different materials, such as concrete, asphalt, wood, and metal. Packaging and product descriptions of the best ice melts will reveal what materials they can be used on safely, so be sure to read this information prior to purchase. It would be unwise to apply a product that could corrode concrete, rust metal, or damage wood on those surfaces around the home.

The quest for comfort and convenience in frigid weather has led to the invention of such products as heated jackets, heated gloves, and electric snow shovels. Similarly, certain ice melts have been developed to work in colder climates. Some products won’t work in temperatures lower than 20 degrees Fahrenheit. This is acceptable if the temperature in an area seldom gets that low, but these products won’t get the job done if you live in a colder spot. For locations where temperatures can reach less than 20 degrees Fahrenheit, you’ll want to purchase a product specifically made for lower temperatures.

The time it takes a product to melt ice and snow depends on several factors. Liquid ice melters and self-heating ice melters act fairly quickly. Unlike solid melters that take time to absorb moisture and create the brine, liquid products are already a brine. Self-heating ice melters have a similar advantage: Instead of absorbing moisture, the pellets will heat up more quickly and melt the ice and snow faster than other ice melters. Regardless of which form you choose, there will still be some downtime while you wait for it to work, which you put to good use cleaning your windows with an ice scraper.

Longevity refers to an ice melt’s ability to keep working beyond the initial application period. A long-lasting ice melter is especially helpful when snowstorms or icy rain continue throughout the day. Although long-lasting ice melt tends to be more expensive, the cost can even out since smaller amounts of product tend to get the job done.

The chemicals in some ice melters can be hazardous to pets and plants. According to Alex Blutinger, Medical Director of Veterinary Emergency Group in Greenwich, Connecticut, “Melting ice can be very dangerous to animals, specifically because of the harsh ingredients in ice melt products. Ingestion of these chemicals can cause stomach upset, vomiting, and diarrhea. It may also irritate the paw pads and exposed areas of the limbs.” Dr. Blutinger says that, if you suspect your pet has been exposed to unsafe deicing chemicals, you should wipe your pet’s paws with a damp cloth or baby wipe to minimize ingestion through liking and reduce the risk of skin irritation. While using a pet-safe ice melt is smart, you can also reduce exposure using paw was or booties.

Certain elements in ice melters can also do environmental damage, such as killing wildlife that may ingest the pellets or aquatic life if the chemicals reach waterways. Many people are concerned about the impact of using large amounts of these products outdoors, so it’s important to read product information carefully to understand the dos and don’ts of using ice melt.

To ensure you get the best performance out of your purchase (or even a homemade ice melt), try the following de-icing tips and tricks.

If you’re not keen to try to melt ice without salt and want more information about ice melts, here are answers to some commonly asked questions.

Ice melters absorb moisture and create a brine that then melts snow and ice. This eventually breaks the bond between the ice and the surface, creating a slush.

Generally speaking, calcium chloride is better for ice melt. It’s effective at low temperatures, is a good choice for concrete, and comes in pellet, granule, and liquid forms. #7581. Is a Reverse Osmosis Filter System Actually Worth It? We Break Down Every Cost

What’s lurking in your water? RO filters get rid of everything from microplastics to heavy metals, but are they overkill?

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

In this installment of Home 2.0, we dive into reverse osmosis filtration for the kitchen, its benefits and hidden costs — plus which households should invest in the technology, and who can skip it.

I’ve lived in some places with questionable drinking water. One town issued a notice that the municipal water supply had experienced a sewage incident. Another had an arsenic problem. I’ve also lived on well water, with concerns of contamination from nearby agricultural fields.

My solution used to be buying five-gallon jugs of spring water. But that was costly and a hassle, so six years ago, I switched to an under-sink reverse osmosis (RO) filter for my drinking and cooking water.

Under-sink RO filters work like this: water passes through a series of filters, including an RO membrane, which removes dissolved substances — including lead, arsenic, nitrates, forever chemicals, chlorine, fluoride and sediment — down to 0.0001 microns. The cleaned water then comes out through a faucet, installed near the sink.

“Reverse osmosis provides the safest level of drinking water possible,” says international water filtration specialist Andrew D. Daily. “It strips out 100% of bacteria, cysts, dissolved solids, chlorine, rust, viruses and microplastics.”

But RO systems are also a considerable investment. So, we asked a range of health and plumbing experts for their thoughts on who should get an RO system, plus how to pick the right one. Ahead is what they said, how much RO systems cost up front and over time, and whether it’s worth the upgrade.

RO water systems range from a few hundred dollars to over $1,000. The good news is that if you have basic plumbing knowledge and are comfortable drilling a hole in your countertop, installing one can be a DIY task. Otherwise, pro installation usually runs upwards of $300, not including add-ons like a refrigerator/ice-maker connection, leak protection, an additional electric outlet and other plumbing modifications.

The biggest downside to RO systems is that they waste water. For every gallon that comes out of the faucet, somewhere between one-half and four gallons get flushed down the drain through the filtration process. That means if you use 5 gallons of water a day for cooking and drinking, the RO system wastes between 2.5 and 20 gallons.

Over a year, that adds up to between 500 and 8,500 gallons, depending on your RO system. On the low end, that’s only a few pennies more on your yearly water utility bill, but on the high end, it could be close to $100.

Some RO water systems also require electricity. The amount of power they consume varies by model, but usually falls between 20 and 40 watts per hour. Since RO systems typically run for less than an hour a day, even if you live in a place with high electricity rates, they should add only a few dollars a year to your electricity bill.

Maintaining RO systems is an easy DIY task, though some people choose to pay a pro to keep track of it for them. Expect to spend roughly the following for DIY maintenance:

Daily recommends buying only name-brand filters, even though they’re more expensive. “Name brands follow strict regulations,” he says. ”Generic China-based deals often do not provide the same protection.”

A quality RO system can last 10 years or longer with proper maintenance. “Many parts, including filters, membranes, faucets and tanks can be replaced individually,” says plumbing expert Danielle Smith. “Once a system gets older, though, replacement may make more sense than repeated repairs.”

“The biggest thing for me is convenience,” says environmental and wellness expert Helen Christoni, who has an AquaTru system. “We use water all day long, drinking it, cooking with it and filling water bottles. Once installed, it just became part of my kitchen and my family’s daily health.”

Herman Hartanto, founder of Tampa Fast Home Buyer, has a Waterdrop G3P600 in his kitchen ($429 retail). It’s a tankless model, a feature he appreciates since it takes up minimal cabinet space. He also likes the display with real-time reports on total dissolved solids (TDS) and filter health. His only complaint is the occasional noise it generates. “The pump that draws the water on demand makes quite loud noise, which I can feel clearly at night when everything is silent,” he says.

Personally, I’ve used two RO filter systems. My first one was an iSpring, which I chose because of its affordability. It worked well, but like Hartanto, I found the pump noisy (even though mine had a water-holding tank). My second one, which I’ve only recently installed, is a Waterdrop X12 Pro, which I chose to upgrade to because of its water-saving efficiency, ability to add calcium and magnesium back into the water, clear display and range of other premium features. So far, I’ve found it to be quiet, efficient, and free of quirks (though at $1,400 off-sale, the price is a bit of a shocker).

Depending on what type of contaminants you have in your water, there are several alternatives to an under-sink RO water filter:

“Find out what’s in your water before buying anything,” says Smith. “Don’t choose a system based only on how many stages it has or how many contaminants the box says it removes. Instead, start with your water and choose the system around what you actually need.”

If you’re worried about contaminants like microplastics, arsenic, lead, forever chemicals, pesticides and pharmaceuticals, then an RO filter is a good choice.

“Water quality can vary tremendously depending on where you live, and even your home’s plumbing can affect what ultimately comes out of your faucet,” says Christoni. “Reverse osmosis addresses such a broad range of contaminants, and with an under-sink system, that purified water is available all day long without having to think about it.”

For Daily, the biggest reason to invest in a RO system is microplastics. “The amount of microplastics found in human brains, blood and organs have been increasing yearly,” he says. “Although there is not enough information to prove a detrimental effect on our health, many of my clients choose a cautious approach to water treatment.”

Otherwise, Daily says that RO filters are overkill in most U.S. cities, where tap water is generally considered safe. Even in Mexico, where water is often contaminated, he usually recommends sticking with under-sink ultrafiltration systems, since they’re a fraction of the cost, don’t waste water and don’t require power or space for a reservoir.

If you’re currently buying bottled water, then yes, an RO system will soon pay for itself. But, otherwise, it really just depends on what you want to remove from your water. If you have arsenic, nitrates, salts, microplastics, fluoride, sulfates and other dissolved solids (TDS), RO systems are a great solution.

Otherwise, a less-expensive ultrafiltration system might be a better choice. Either way, having an under-sink filtration system is a good way to ensure your family has access to clean water, both on a daily basis and after flooding events and other natural disasters that contaminate city and well water.

Get the JMEXSUSS indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

The Lidore indoor string lights go back to basics with white wire and traditional incandescent bulbs. Designed so that the entire string will stay lit if one of the traditional incandescent bulbs goes out, the set includes two replacement bulbs. However, these lights may not last as long as standard LEDs, especially if used constantly over several weeks.

Get the Lidore indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

All 200 of these warm white and multicolored LED lights are remote controlled, can be used indoors and outdoors, and come with 11 lighting modes to provide any ambience desired. Plus, these lights come with four different dimmer settings to emit a warm glow or bright spectacle.

To make Christmas morning even more relaxing, shoppers can rely on the 26.25-foot range of the remote control for quick adjustments and the programmable timer so the lights stay lit as long as needed. Plus, this 82-foot strand of lights can be connected to two other strands of Christmas lights, extending the lighting effects to more than 246 feet.

Get the Brizled LED Christmas lights at Amazon.

These Loende battery-operated string lights provide versatile decor options and reduce presence of wires and cords. The battery pack has a small loop to hide it on wreaths or other decorations.

The Loende lights also come in multicolor and white with a white wire option as well. Each type has eight lighting modes, including combination, slow glow, flash, slow fade, sequential, waves, twinkle, and steady. These lights are waterproof for indoor or outdoor use.

Get the Loende indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

Whether it’s for a 10- to 12-foot tree, a very long stairway banister, or even for hanging around the ceiling, the MZD8391 105-foot Christmas lights can fit the bill. This option has eight different light modes, a copper wire in PVC construction, up to 20,000 hours of life, and LED bulbs to help lower holiday energy consumption. Plus, each of the 300 LED lights stays cool to the touch, no matter how long they are in use.

Made to resemble authentic vintage decorations, these Abeja bubble lights have a retro vibe straight from the 1940s. Each string is 11 feet long and contains eight lights and can connect to an additional 11 sets for a total of 12 strands.

Get the Twinkle Star Christmas lights at Amazon or Target.

Suitable for indoor and outdoor use, the Holiday Essence mini Christmas lights come with 16 feet of LED Christmas lights with more than 60 LED lights per strand for ample light during the holiday season. Get the Holiday Essence Christmas lights at Amazon.

The Louis Choice shatterproof LED bulbs save energy, but they’re also equipped with a built-in timer that runs on a 6-hour-on, 18-hour-off schedule. A 49-foot string provides adequate length to use on a large Christmas tree or banister. However, 16 feet is devoted to the lead wire to help the string reach an outlet.

This model can extend by an additional nine light strings to lengthen its overall reach. A memory feature turns the lights on in the same mode in which they were turned off. The globe portion of the light is attractive, but it’s plastic, which can be quite fragile.

Get the Louis Choice indoor Christmas lights at Amazon.

We researched more than 90 indoor Christmas lights from almost as many brands. Specifically, we looked at user experience, reliability, and durability. LED lights were more likely to make this list because of their energy efficiency and ability to work with smart technology. However, incandescent bulbs also made the list for their soft, warm light and affordability.

Finally, we considered design. Bulbs, both large and small, globe and novelty, made the list, but they had to have the durability and reliability to warrant their inclusion. We tried to represent a wide range of options and brands to fit different preferences.

Everything from the string length to the bulb size and power source can affect the look and feel of Christmas lights. The following considerations are important to take into account before starting to browse for the best indoor Christmas lights for the home.

Traditional incandescent bulbs work by creating enough heat to make a filament inside the bulb light up. Consequently, these lights use a lot of energy and release a significant amount of heat. However, they’re less expensive than LEDs and have a warm white glow that LEDs don’t.

LED Christmas lights have diodes that emit light via the movement of electrons within the semiconductor. LED bulbs are significantly more energy efficient and durable than traditional incandescent bulbs. They also release far less heat. LED bulbs are used in most smart lights, offering up to several million color choices.

Distance to a power source is a concern when buying and installing Christmas lights. For indoor lights, power must come from electricity or batteries. Lights with an electric plug require access to an electrical outlet or an extension cord. Electricity provides consistent power that never runs out (unless the power goes out). Several strings can connect to each other to use power from a single outlet. However, outlets can get crowded with all the light plugs.

Battery-powered Christmas lights are less common, though they are convenient. They can hang almost anywhere without proximity to an outlet. However, battery-powered lights have a short runtime and will dim as the power runs out.

Wire lengths vary from short 10-foot strings to 66- to 100-foot strings. A longer cord means fewer outlets and connection points between strings; however, experts recommend using strings in lengths appropriate for the decor job at hand. Use a tape measure to estimate the distance required to wrap around the tree or run down the banister.

Bulb size should be to scale with the rest of the holiday decor. Delicate ornaments may get overpowered by large bulbs. If unsure of the right size, mini lights blend into the background no matter the style or theme.

White, single-color, and multicolor sum up the Christmas light color options. Whites can be warm (yellowish) or cool (bluish), and single colors can be red, green, blue, orange, purple, and various hues in between. Pick a color or several colors that complement holiday themes. White makes an ideal neutral when unsure of which color to choose.

Shapes range from globes and small teardrop lights to vintage bulbs shaped like candleholders or snowmen. The shape should complement the rest of the decor, just like the color and style.

A few lighting modes include twinkle flash, slow glow, chasing flash, slow fade, and steady on. Smart LED Christmas tree lights offer the most lighting options. Some allow the user to set the colors by section or offer variable brightness adjustments. Lights that feature lighting modes may cost more than a typical string of Christmas lights, especially if they’re smart lights, because they usually cost more.

Choosing the right lights with the perfect length, color, and style isn’t an easy decision. We’ve answered the most common questions to help make your choice easier and get those twinkling Christmas lights up and running.

The Christmas lights used by professionals are usually LED lights with coaxial connectors, which are a little more hard-core than domestic lights. The wiring may be different, but the lights are not.

Color depends on the decor theme and personal preferences. White offers a clean, classic look, while a single color adds mood. Cheerful multicolor lights bring fun to the holidays. Think about the look you want to create, and go with a color that supports your decor.

Incandescent bulbs are approved for safe use on Christmas trees. However, LED Christmas lights don’t get as hot, which probably makes them a safer option for a live tree.

Remove each bulb one at a time, placing a piece of foil in the socket after removing the bulb. If the lights turn back on, you’ve found the bad bulb.

Longevity and durability vary by brand, but incandescent bulbs typically last two or three seasons, and LED bulbs typically last six or seven seasons. Both can last longer if cared for and stored appropriately. Certain conditions, such as living near the ocean or in an area that experiences extreme heat, can shorten their lifespan.

#7579. Court Blocks W. Va. AG's Subpoena to Environmentalist Nonprofits

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Part of the AG's argument was that the nonprofits relied on a climate change scenario, RCP8.5, that has been recently "retired."

From yesterday's decision by Judge Joseph Goodwin (S.D. W. Va.) in W. Va. Rivers Coalition, Inc. v. McCuskey:

The Attorney General of West Virginia has used the State's power to compel two citizen organizations to open ten years of their files: their drafts and internal arguments, the groups they have funded, the people who serve on their boards, the coalitions they have joined, and what they have told the agencies they petition. Neither organization markets goods nor services relevant to the subpoenas. The Attorney General identifies no consumer who was cheated, no sale, and no purchase made in reliance on anything either group said.

What these organizations do is argue in public about what coal, oil, and gas do to West Virginia's waters and climate. The State's chief legal officer, who has publicly condemned that advocacy, now demands to know how they reached their views and who stood with them.

The First Amendment forbids a State from using its investigative power that way, and I will not allow it while this case is pending.

The country was founded on the premise that a citizen owes the government no account of his opinions or of the people he holds them with. The Attorney General has demanded that two citizen organizations hand the State their working lives.

The State wants a decade of what they published, down to a note sent to a single person outside the organization, along with the unreleased drafts and the internal arguments over what to say. He demanded the names of the organizations that fund them and what each gave, and he has now withdrawn that demand. He still wants the groups they paid, the board members they share, the coalitions they joined, and the comments they filed with the agencies they were petitioning. Because the demand period runs to the date of compliance, the subpoenas reach new communications written while they remain outstanding. No demand identifies a consumer, a sale, or a statement anyone relied on. The subpoenas go into how these citizens arrived at their positions on public questions and who helped them get there.

The Plaintiffs in this case, West Virginia Rivers Coalition, Inc. ("WVRC") and 350.org, promote clean waters, reduced carbon emissions, and healthier lives for the people of West Virginia and beyond. They do not sell any service. They do not advertise a certain product of their own. Instead, they promote ideas. Some of that advocacy and some of those ideas are based, in part, on one model. For that, they have been subpoenaed and asked to turn over ten years' worth of information far beyond any use of that one model.

AG McCuskey's actions violate the protections afforded by the United States Constitution. The Plaintiffs, on this record, have only engaged in protected advocacy speech, not commercial speech. The subpoenas issued on the Plaintiffs trespass on their freedom of association, chill their exercise of the First Amendment, and deter others from engaging in similar conduct.

Because Plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits of their claim that the subpoenas violate their First Amendment freedom of association, and because the remaining injunction factors also favor Plaintiffs, their Motion for a Temporary Restraining Order, is GRANTED.

Attorney General McCuskey is enjoined from enforcing these investigative subpoenas for the next fourteen days as set out in the Conclusion of this Memorandum Opinion and Order….

Plaintiff WVRC is a river advocacy nonprofit corporation organized under the laws of West Virginia, and its "mission is to promote clean and healthy West Virginia waters for all." The nonprofit is committed to "clean water and healthy rivers through research, public education, policy advocacy, citizen water-quality monitoring, and engagement with state and federal agencies." It has a modest staff of 15 and an annual budget of approximately $2 million primarily funded by foundations and other organizations. WVRC regularly submits comments on proposed legislation, permits, and rules concerning water quality. And as this court is familiar, WVRC is a party litigant in multiple cases across the Fourth Circuit that challenge permits and approvals for infrastructure projects, pipeline projects, injection wells, and toxic discharges. Because of its litigation efforts, WVRC coordinates "with other organizations through shared counsel" about litigation strategy.

WVRC also engages in public education and information campaigns, including "statements about the effects of climate change in West Virginia's waters and communities, and about the environmental effects of fossil-fuel extraction, transport, and combustion." It is a member of multiple different coalitions committed to similar goals. To fund ts work, WVRC "solicits charitable contributions from the public through its website, mailings, emails, and events," but it does not publish the identities of its funders.

Plaintiff 350.org is a nonprofit corporation, and its "mission is to build a grassroots movement to end the use of fossil fuels and to accelerate the transition to renewable energy." The organization publishes information about climate change, organizes public demonstrations, and coordinates with other organizations with similar goals. 350.org also "solicits charitable contributions from the public through grant applications and through its website, mailings, emails, and events." Those grants and contributions are subject to opt-in confidentiality in some cases and agreed upon confidentiality in other cases.

And an excerpt from the court's First Amendment analysis (for more on RCP8.5, see this N.Y. Times article):

[T]he Court applies "exacting scrutiny" to compelled disclosures of protected First Amendment speech and association. To be a permissible intrusion on the First Amendment, "there must be 'a substantial relation between the disclosure requirement and a sufficiently important governmental interest.'" …

The subpoenas … "… concern[ ] an investigation into alleged unfair or deceptive acts or practices and other possible violations of the West Virginia Consumer Credit and Protection Act ('WVCCPA')." State code authorizes the Attorney General, if he "has probable cause," to "subpoena witnesses, compel their attendance, adduce evidence, and require the production of any matter which is relevant to the investigation."

Under West Virginia law, "[u]nfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce are … unlawful." Trade or commerce "means the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of any goods or services and shall include any trade or commerce, directly or indirectly, affecting the people of this state." "Unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices" includes 16 different definitions including "[e]ngaging in any other conduct which similarly creates a likelihood of confusion or of misunderstanding."

Deploying these broad definitions, AG McCuskey's theory is that the Plaintiffs, environmental advocacy groups, published information, made comments, and advocated based on a study, the RCP8.5, that has been determined "implausible." According to AG McCuskey, this reliance, and subsequent advocacy, is a deceptive act or practice that affects the energy marketplace of West Virginia.

Begin with common sense—in what way could WVRC and 350.org violate the WVCCPA? They are not financial institutions, lenders, or creditors. They are not businesses seeking to make a profit by engaging with consumers. In fact, both are 501(c)(3) nonprofit organizations. They do not sell services of any kind. As explained, Plaintiffs are advocacy organizations committed to climate issues. Their missions are public education, dissemination of information, advocacy in support of their ideals, and public support of those who align with their beliefs. What little items they sell are merchandise bearing their names and logos. Surely these minimal sales from advocacy organizations are not the transactions the West Virginia legislature sought to protect consumers from….

Plaintiffs do not engage in commercial speech. By virtue of their missions as nonprofit environmental advocacy groups, their interests are not economic. Their interests include public education, funding environmental projects, modeling and projecting the effects of climate change, and contributing to a society that values clean air, clean water, and healthier lives. The fact that their advocacy touches on the economy is insufficient to be commercial speech. Therefore, Plaintiffs' protected speech and advocacy alleged in this case cannot be regulated under the WVCCPA.

Accordingly, I find that the WVCCPA cannot supply a "sufficiently important governmental interest" under the "exacting scrutiny" applied to freedom of association claims. I next turn to the severity of the "disclosure requirement" under the "exacting scrutiny" analysis….

As discussed, the subpoenas broadly assert that a violation of the WVCCPA might have occurred. And in his response, AG McCuskey admits that there may not be any WVCCPA violation. He does, however, have authority to issue subpoenas to investigate "whether a violation … has, in fact, occurred."

That violation, AG McCuskey argues, arises from only a few instances of Plaintiffs using a certain climate projection model, RCP8.5. Any publication born from that model, he asserts, is potentially unfair or deceptive. So to assess the breadth of the subpoenas and the compelled disclosure Plaintiffs are subjected to, the court turns to the subpoenas' demands. It is reasonable to assume that the demands would roughly track the RCP8.5-related violations and the allegations of unfair or deceptive trade practices.

Not so. The subpoenas ask for much more. The 16 categories of demands include every statement Plaintiffs have ever published about a West Virginia energy business with a "Climate Claim." But that demand is not limited to climate-related statements supported by the RCP8.5 model. It includes every climate-related statement that names a West Virginia energy business which is published and supported or informed, at least in part, by any model, study, project, plan, projection, or paper. Demand No. 4 is similarly broad: the subpoena demands every published projection concerning West Virginia and all documents related to those projections, without narrowing it down to those supported by the RCP8.5.

The rest of the demands do not even try to mask their broad and sweeping intentions. Donation requests, payments to third parties, and licensing and funding documents of all projects concerning West Virginia are demanded. Every document projecting costs and damages is demanded, as well as every report, study, model, or paper that the Plaintiffs directly or indirectly supported. Documents pertaining to internal considerations are demanded wholesale. So, too, are all documents pertaining to third-party communication and coordination in any fashion. And even with AG McCuskey's last-minute withdrawal of certain demands for donor information, Plaintiffs will still be obligated to disclose "board affiliation, coalition partners, grantees, agency submissions, internal deliberations and drafts, solicitation totals and targeting."

Plaintiffs call this a fishing expedition. In part, I agree. The subpoenas demand a large share of documents in Plaintiffs' control for the last ten years. But even on a fishing expedition, hoping to just get one bite in the vast and quiet water, a person brings a fishing pole. And in other cases, perhaps, a net. Here, AG McCuskey has abandoned both the fishing pole and the net. Instead, he has brought dynamite to the lake. Tossing a couple in, he hopes to catch something.

As stated, compelled disclosure that invades First Amendment protections can only stand if there is a substantial relation between what must be disclosed and a "sufficiently important governmental interest." Here, I find neither a sufficiently important government interest nor do I find a substantial relationship between the compelled disclosure and the government interest….

And the court also briefly notes plaintiffs' retaliation claim, without resolving it:

Plaintiffs have alleged substantial evidence to support their [retaliation] claim. AG McCuskey has publicly disparaged pro-environmental groups and has called for the DOJ to investigate similar groups. He has joined contentious litigation against environmental advocacy organizations. And the chasm between the subpoenas' demands and the purported basis for investigation suggests a retaliatory motive.

This phenomenon of state and federal investigation into the affairs of advocacy non-profits has begun to permeate our culture. The courts have enjoined civil investigative demands on comparable records. [Citations omitted. -EV]

However, because retaliation concerns the Attorney General's motive, I will reserve judgment on Count One until he can present evidence at a hearing for a preliminary injunction. Having already determined that an injunction is warranted on the basis of Count Two (freedom of association), the court declines to address the remaining counts….

Derek Teaney and Amanda Demmerle (Appalachian Mountain Advocates, Inc.) represent plaintiffs.

NEXT: Short Circuit: An inexhaustive weekly compendium of rulings from the federal courts of appeal

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7577. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

#7576. Step Up Your Game With a DIY Folding Step Stool

This weekend project walks you through every cut and joint to make a foldable step stool you’ll actually use every day.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

Turn leftover hardwood scraps into a rock-solid folding step stool that puts wobbly plastic versions to shame.

At some point in our lives we will need a folding step stool. You know, the one that stays out of the way but, gives you that little extra boost when you don’t need a full step ladder. In my case, I find myself reaching for a step stool more often than I’d like to admit especially when trying to reach into a work truck. When I need something, I prefer to make it and am happy to share the steps with you. Just because it is small doesn’t mean it isn’t as satisfying to make – enjoy!

On the miter saw and/or table saw, cut the top step (A), all four legs (B), the guides (C), ad the bottom crossbrace (E). Set aside everything but the legs (B) until later.

Using a compass with a pencil, draw 1-1/2-inch diameter half-circles at the bottom of each leg (B) to match the 1/2-inch width of the leg.

Use a disc or belt sander with a coarse-grit sandpaper (80 or 100-grit) to shape the ends of the legs by sanding up to the marked pencil lines for your arch. Once you have sanded to the line, work your way up to 220-grit sandpaper for a smoother finish.

Using a router table or a router equipped with a 1/4-inch round-over bit, round over all the edges of the step (A) and all four legs (B). Be sure to use clamps to hold the pieces while making your passes with the router.

With all the parts machined, sand all the components to 220 grit and apply a couple of coats of a wood finish of your choice. Allow the finish to dry before moving on to assembly.

Spread wood glue in hole 3 at the top of each inside leg (B). Insert the ends of the 3/4-in. dowel cross brace (D) and tap the legs on with a rubber mallet until D is fully seated.

Set the 1-1/4-in.-square cross brace (E) between the bottoms of the legs, with its bottom edge 2-1/8 in. up from the bottom of the legs. To keep the legs parallel while you drill, clamp a scrap the same length as the cross brace (E) between them at mid-height. Check for square.

Using hole 4 in each leg as a guide, drill a 1/2-in. hole about 1 in. deep into the center of each end of the cross brace (E). Glue 1/2-in. dowels, cut longer than the holes are deep, and drive them through the legs with a mallet until they bottom out in the cross brace (E).

Lock each of the four joints with a single brad nail through the leg into the dowel. Trim the protruding ends of all the dowels flush with a pull saw.

Flip the top step (A) upside down. Position the guide rails (C) 1/2-in. in from each side and centered front to back, leaving 1-1/2-in. at the front and back. Trace around each rail.

Drill two 1/4-in. holes, 3/4-in. deep, centered on each outline. Keep the bit plumb when drilling (or drill at the drill press).

Insert dowel centers in the holes. Align each rail with its outline and press down to mark the hole locations. Drill matching 1/4-in. holes in the rails, about 7/8-in. deep. That’s slightly deeper than the dowel needs, which leaves room for glue.

Glue and insert 1/4-in x 1-1/2-in. dowels and secure the guide rails (C) to the step (A).

Thread 1/4-inch x 3-1/2-inch carriage bolts through hole 1 in the center of the legs to connect an outside leg to the outside of each of the connected inside legs. Put a washer between each pair of legs and secure with a nylon lock nut on the inside of the inside legs.

Connect the two outside legs (B) to the sides of the guide rails (C) by threading 1/4-inch x 2-1/2-inch pan head screws through hole 5 in the guide rails and through hole 2 on the outside legs. Use a washer on the outside of the guide rails and pliers to hold the nylon lock nuts while you tighten them into the 5/8-inch countersunk holes.

The strap acts as a stop, limiting how far the legs can open. Wrap one end of an upholstery strap around the middle of the top cross brace (D) and staple it in place with a narrow-crown stapler. Open the stool until the seat sits level, then pull the strap snug and staple the other end centered on the underside of the top step (A). Use several 1/2-in. staples at each end so the strap holds securely.

A step stool should be about 11 to 16-in. wide to fit both feet comfortably side by side. For a portable or compact version, stay toward the narrow end of that range.

A single-step stool should be 6 to 9-in. tall. That’s a good height for reaching into a truck bed, helping kids reach a tall bathroom sink, or getting to the top pantry shelves.

#7575. A Libertarian Perspective on the 2026 Election

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Why we should vote "Democrat by Default" for federal offices - with a few rare exceptions. I build on a post by political philosopher Dan Shapiro.

I was going to write a post about why, in this election, the right thing for libertarians to do is vote for Democrats for all federal offices, unless either 1) the Dem candidate is DSA, or 2) the GOP candidate is one of those very rare Republicans who oppose all or most of Trump's awful policies. But libertarian political philosopher Dan Shapiro beat me to it, in an excellent post at the Bleeding Heart Libertarian substack. I agree with the vast bulk of what he says. But I have a few additions and caveats that I will append after quoting a few key passages from Dan's post. Before getting into detail, I will note that I generally believe in voting for the lesser evil among those candidates with a realistic chance to win. Thus, unlike Dan, I don't usually vote for third party candidates, even in more normal times. If you're opposed to "lesser evil" voting on principle, we have a disagreement that goes  far beyond the present election. But I would urge you to check out my defense of that practice, where I explain why you should even vote for the evil Queen Cersei over the even more evil Sauron, if those are the only available choices.

I don't expect this post or Dan's will change the outcome of the election. They almost certainly won't. But they might still be helpful in thinking through big issues we face in the current political moment.

Most of my voting life I voted for the Libertarian Party when they advocated classical liberal/libertarian policies. Now those who care about and prioritize liberty and a free society—however they label themselves—should vote Democratic unless the candidate is a Democratic Socialist….

There's been so much criminality and misdeeds in the Trump administration that it's exhausting to cover it all, but keeping "the land of the free and the home of the brave" means remembering the essentials. I provide links when the points I make are not common knowledge and/or might be controversial.

January 6: Trump is the only presidential candidate in the US who refused to concede that he lost. He told a crowd to "fight like hell," and the mob then stormed the Capitol to try to overturn the results. The House impeached him for "incitement of insurrection," and 57 senators, including seven Republicans, voted to convict—short of the two-thirds required. After his campaign of lies and deception and pressuring election officials to falsify the results failed to overturn the election, he later pardoned all the perpetrators of the violence.

ICE: masked secret police who kidnap people and send them to hellholes in El Salvador, where they were subject to constant beatings, sexual abuse, and torture; to the Central African Republic, in the midst of a brutal civil war with severe human rights abuses; to Florida's "Alligator Alcatraz," where large numbers of detainees were held in cages the size of phone booths; and to Fort Bliss, Texas, where guards grabbed detainees' testicles while beating them. There've been zero consequences for this; indeed, Trump says they are "immune."

Not only were the deportations done without any notification to families or lawyers, but ICE has disappeared from databases those they seized so lawyers and families can't find them.

ICE and CBP have rammed people in their cars, dragged the occupants out, and rammed into houses without warrants. They have murdered, wounded, and assaulted protestors and ICE monitors—Alex Pretti and Renee Good, during the ICE occupation of Minneapolis, being the most publicized—but there have been many others.

There is now "expedited removal" for anyone undocumented, which means no hearing before a judge. (And this is even though immigration judges are—wrongly—a part of, and not independent of, the executive branch.) Indeed, Trump fired any immigration judge who disagreed with him or whom he perceived as not being deportation-friendly enough, and replaced the Board of Immigration Appeals, which has denied appeals for almost all deportation orders.

The administration removed TPS (temporary protected status) for immigrants fleeing violence and is deporting them to the very countries the State Department has declared unsafe—e.g., Haiti.

ICE apprehended immigrant parents after they dropped their kids off at school (see here, here, and here), as well as apprehending children and toddlers and using them as bait (the Liam Conejo Ramos incident)….

Trump sent Marines to LA, and National Guard troops to Chicago and DC. This violates a basic norm since the Founding and violates Posse Comitatus, a statute banning the military from policing.

Trump and FCC chairman Carr threatened talk shows and networks for dissenting political opinions.

As mentioned, ICE murdered, assaulted, and wounded protestors and ICE monitors.

The administration targeted people for their political views and for writing op-eds. Rochester resident David Streever sent a critical email to the director of ICE, and five months later, federal officers tracked his movements and staked out his New York City hotel as he returned from an overseas trip….

There is much more, including explanations of why the Democrats (with the notable exception of DSA types) are far less bad than this, despite their considerable flaws. I myself have written about the evils of the DSA here, explaining why they are comparable to MAGA nationalist Republicans.  In addition to the harm individual DSA members might cause if elected to office, it is important to reduce their numbers as much as possible, so as to minimize the chances that socialists could take over the Democratic Party, as MAGA nationalists have done with the GOP.

I have a few additions to Dan's arguments.

First, it is essential to consider the enormous scale of Trump's harmful and unjust immigration and trade policies. When it comes to setting issue priorities, scale matters a great deal. Even under normal administrations, immigration restrictions threaten the economic and civil liberties of American citizens (to say nothing of those of immigrants themselves) more than any other federal policy. Trump's vast expansion of exclusion and mass deportation has made things a lot worse. The liberty and well-being of millions of people are at stake.

Trump's trade policies seek to impose the highest tariff levels since those that gravely exacerbated the Great Depression, and also are a grave menace to the rule of law. Here too, we're talking about massive effects on the liberty and welfare of millions. Judicial review can and has helped curb these abuses (more on the tariff front than immigration). But there is much Congress can do to help, including curbing funding to ICE and other agencies complicit in wrongdoing. Congressional Democrats also plan to cut back executive tariff authority. That may not succeed while Trump remains in office, but can help set the stage for later progress.

Dan raises the issue of whether non-DSA Democrats might be worse than the Trump-era GOP on economic liberty issues. This becomes an easy issue if you recognize that immigration restrictions and tariffs are also violations of economic liberty. Due to their massive scale, Trump's actions in this area easily outweigh the very real economic policy flaws of non-DSA Dems. And then we have such things as his acquisition of federal government stakes in numerous private firms, something that even the most left-wing recent Democratic presidents didn't attempt. It's a dramatic example of how MAGA nationalists have dangerous economic policies similar to those of socialists.

It is also important to remember that a Democratic Senate could block Trump's horrible executive and judicial nominees. I don't want to see any more Pete Hegseths and RFK, Jrs. In Trump's first term, he had some good judicial nominees. In the second, he has mostly  bad ones (Emil Bove is a particularly egregious example). From a libertarian perspective, I'd rather have a standard liberal nominee fill the next Supreme Court vacancy (despite all the flaws such jurists have) than the type of right-winger Trump II is all too likely to nominate. Such a person would probably be selected for his willingness to turn a blind eye to executive abuses of power, trample civil liberties, and bulldoze constitutional obstacles to MAGA nationalist policies, such as federalism and separation of powers. There may well not be any Supreme Court vacancies, of course. But lower court nominations will arise, and they matter too.

Finally, I'm more hawkish than the average libertarian, and I think it's important to counter Trump's policies of undermining the Western alliance, and coddling mass-murdering dictators like Vladimir Putin and (to a lesser extent) Xi Jinping. We should care about defending liberty worldwide, not just in one country, especially since the two are interconnected. The Democrats (except for a few far-leftists) oppose this awfulness and could use control of Congress to help curb it.

In these and other areas, a Democratic-controlled Congress could not fully stop Trump's abuses. The executive has accumulated too much power for that, often in constitutionally dubious ways. But congressional control of nominations and purse strings can do much to constrain the executive at the margin. And electoral repudiation of Trump's abuses can reduce the risk that future presidents will imitate them.

I do have a few caveats to attach to Dan's otherwise compelling points:

First, Dan doesn't differentiate between elections for federal offices and those for state and local ones. I do. Beating the GOP in federal races is vital for countering Trump's awful agenda. At the state and local level, other issues are dominant, and Republicans are often better than Dems on the crucial issues of housing, state-level taxation, and state and local economic regulation. Which party is better on these and other state and local issues will vary from state to state. For example, red state Republicans are much better on the crucial issue of housing deregulation than blue state ones (who often back exclusionary zoning against Democratic reform efforts). Thus, it might make sense to vote for Republican candidates in some state and local races, but not others, depending on the issues involved.

Second, when it comes to the DSA problem, there can be difficult questions about what to do with Dem candidates who are not actual DSA members, but seem closely adjacent to them. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is a notable example. He says he's not a socialist, but also is closely aligned with socialists like Bernie Sanders, and "influencer" Hasan Piker, the guy who - among other things - praises communist mass murderers like Mao Zedong.

In this post, I'm not going to try to adjudicate each individual candidate and race. I will merely say that if you're trying to figure out whether a non-DSA member is actually a socialist, two noteworthy indicators are 1) whether he or she supports government control of all or most of the economy and 2) whether they praise socialist despots abroad, such as Mao, Fidel Castro, and others. If the answers to one or both questions are "yes," that's a strong indication they might be socialists, and therefore not worth voting for, except perhaps against the very worst Republicans.

There is a similar calculation in identifying the few Republicans who have opposed Trump's worst policies. Here, key indicators are whether they have opposed his tariffs, his mass deportations, his kowtowing to Vladimir Putin, and his attacks on civil liberties. Sadly, Republican candidates with consistent strong records on all or most of these issues, are few and far between, though Republican criticism of the tariffs and policies towards Russia have picked up in recent weeks.

Finally, as Dan would agree, voting for Democratic candidates does not imply supporting everything the Democratic Party does, or abstaining from criticizing Democrats on the many occasions when they do bad things.

Elsewhere, I have argued that libertarians, in the current political moment, should seek an alliance with "abundance liberals." But alliance is not the same thing as total agreement. And the Democratic Party obviously includes various factions who are much worse than the abundance types. We should keep that in mind, even as we recognize that right now the Republicans are much worse.

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7573. What Is “Heart Attack Snow,” and Why Is It So Dangerous?

Heavy, wet snow can turn an ordinary winter chore into a health risk. Learn why people call it heart attack snow and how to shovel safely.

Shoveling snow can be a dangerous winter chore. Icy walkways can cause serious falls, and prolonged exposure to the cold can lead to hypothermia or frostbite. Another safety concern is something called “heart attack snow.”

The name sounds dramatic, but it points to a real concern for people clearing sidewalks and driveways in winter. For those in snowy climates, understanding the risks of heart attack snow is important before picking up a shovel.

Understanding the risks can help prevent a routine chore from becoming a medical emergency.

Heart attack snow is a nickname for heavy, wet snow that’s harder to shovel than dry, powdery snow. The name comes from the strain that lifting this type of snow can place on the heart. According to the National Weather Service, snow with a higher water content weighs more, making each shovelful harder to lift.

The added effort can quickly raise heart rate and blood pressure. Cold temperatures also cause blood vessels to narrow, making the heart work harder. The American Heart Association warns that this combination can trigger a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest.

The association says the risks are especially concerning for “people who already have cardiovascular risks like a sedentary lifestyle or obesity,” including those with a history of smoking, diabetes, high cholesterol, or high blood pressure. People who have previously suffered a heart attack or stroke also face greater risks.

Even lighter, powdery snow can be dangerous, especially when large amounts require repeated lifting or hours of clearing.

Before heading outside, people should warm up indoors and stretch gently. Dressing in layers helps protect against the cold, while staying hydrated is important even when someone doesn’t feel thirsty.

The American Heart Association recommends pushing snow rather than lifting it whenever possible. When lifting is necessary, smaller loads and frequent breaks can help limit physical strain. A snow blower can also reduce the amount of lifting, although operating one still requires effort.

Slippery surfaces are another concern. “Walking on ice is extremely dangerous,” according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The agency recommends using rock salt or another de-icing product to keep walkways clear of ice. Sand can also help prevent slipping.

People with heart disease or significant cardiovascular risk factors should have someone else handle snow removal, according to the American Heart Association.

Recognizing the warning signs of a heart attack is equally important. Chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, dizziness, nausea, cold sweats, or discomfort in the arms, back, or jaw can all signal a serious problem. Symptoms aren’t always severe and can vary from person to person.

Anyone experiencing possible heart attack symptoms should stop shoveling immediately and call 911. The American Heart Association advises against waiting to see whether symptoms go away.

American Heart Association, “Snow Shoveling, Cold Temperatures Combine for Perfect Storm of Heart Health Hazards” American Heart Association, “Warning Signs of a Heart Attack” National Weather Service, “Winter Weather Preparedness” Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, “Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm”
