#7567. Trump vs. WSJ Libel Lawsuit over Trump's Alleged Birthday Wishes to Epstein Thrown out

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court concludes that Trump hadn't adequately alleged facts supporting a showing that the Journal published the article knowing that it was likely false.

From Judge Darrin Gayles (S.D. Fla.) in Trump v. Dow Jones & Co., Inc.:

Those who won our independence believed … that public discussion is a political duty; and that this should be a fundamental principle of the American government. They recognized the risks to which all human institutions are subject. But they knew that order cannot be secured merely through fear of punishment for its infraction; that it is hazardous to discourage thought, hope and imagination; that fear breeds repression; that repression breeds hate; that hate menaces stable government; that the path of safety lies in the opportunity to discuss freely supposed grievances and proposed remedies; and that the fitting remedy for evil counsels is good ones. Believing in the power of reason as applied through public discussion, they eschewed silence coerced by law—the argument of force in its worst form. Recognizing the occasional tyrannies of governing majorities, they amended the Constitution so that free speech and assembly should be guaranteed.

New York Times Co. v. Sullivan (1964) (quoting Whitney v. California (1927) (Brandeis, J., concurring)).

Justice Brandeis's words, as relevant today as they were nearly a century ago, formed the "background" behind the Supreme Court's holding in Sullivan: the First Amendment "prohibits a public [figure] from recovering damages for a defamatory falsehood … unless he proves that the statement was made with actual malice[.]" This constitutional protection is not limited to post-discovery motions and trial. Because "[t]he costs and efforts required to defend a lawsuit through [discovery] could chill free speech nearly as effectively as the absence of the actual malice standard altogether[,]" a public figure plaintiff must plausibly allege actual malice at the outset of the litigation.

This Order addresses President Donald J. Trump's second attempt to plead that Defendants … acted with actual malice when they published an article in the Wall Street Journal … linking him to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein …. As with his first attempt, he has failed. Therefore, for the reasons below, … President Trump's Amended Complaint is dismissed with prejudice….

On July 15, 2025, Palazzolo emailed then White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt ("Leavitt") advising her that Dow Jones intended to publish an article (the "Article") about a birthday letter that President Trump purportedly created for Epstein (the "Letter"). President Trump and his team responded quickly. Leavitt called Palazzolo and told him that the "subject matter" of the proposed Article was false. President Trump, through counsel, denied writing the Letter and warned Dow Jones not to publish the story. {President Trump also denied writing the Letter in an interview before publication.} And President Trump directly told Murdoch that he had not signed or sent the Letter. When Murdoch responded that he would "handle it," President Trump thought the WSJ would not print the Article. Two days later, the WSJ online edition published the Article.

The title of the Article—"Jeffrey Epstein's Friends Sent Him Bawdy Letters for a 50th Birthday Album. One was from Donald Trump"—is in bold print, with a subtitle below reading "[t]he leather-bound book was compiled by Ghislaine Maxwell. The president says the letter 'is a fake thing.'" Leading with a picture of President Trump with Epstein, the Article states the following, in pertinent part:

It was Jeffrey Esptein's 50th birthday, and Ghislaine Maxwell was preparing a special gift to mark the occasion. She turned to Epstein's family and friends. One of them was Donald Trump.

Maxwell collected letters from Trump and dozens of Epstein's other associates for a 2003 birthday album, according to documents reviewed by The Wall Street Journal.

Pages from the leather-bound album—assembled before Epstein was first arrested in 2006—are among the documents examined by Justice Department officials who investigated Epstein and Maxwell years ago, according to people who have reviewed the pages. It's unclear if any of the pages are part of the Trump Administration's recent review….

The letter bearing Trump's name, which was reviewed by the Journal, is bawdy—like others in the album. It contains several lines of typewritten text framed by the outline of a naked woman, which appears to be hand-drawn with a heavy marker. A pair of small arcs denotes the woman's breasts, and the future president's signature is a squiggly "Donald" below her waist, mimicking pubic hair.

The letter concludes: "Happy Birthday—and may every day be another wonderful secret."

In an interview with the Journal on Tuesday evening, Trump denied writing the letter or drawing the picture. "This is not me. This is a fake thing. It's a fake Wall Street Journal story," he said.

"I never wrote a picture in my life. I don't draw pictures of women," he said. "It's not my language. It's not my words."

He told the Journal he was preparing to file a lawsuit if it published an article. "I'm gonna sue The Wall Street Journal just like I sued everyone else," he said….

Justice Department officials didn't respond to requests for comment or address questions about whether the Trump page and other pages of the birthday album were part of the agency's recent documents review. The FBI declined to comment….

Among those who submitted letters were billionaire Leslie Wexner and attorney Alan Dershowitz … Wexner declined to comment through a spokesman … Dershowitz, who represented Epstein after his first arrest, said, "It's been a long time and I don't recall the content of what I may have written….

The book was put together by a New York City bookbinder, Herbert Weitz, according to people who were involved in the process. Weitz, who died in 2020, listed Epstein as a client on his website in 2003.

It isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared. Inside the outline of the naked woman was a typewritten note styled as an imaginary conversation between Trump and Epstein, written in the third person.

When he turned 50, Epstein was already wealthy from managing Wexner's fortune and was socializing with Trump, Clinton and other powerful people. He often entertained at this Manhattan townhouse, Palm Beach, Fla., home and private Caribbean island….

Epstein and Trump spent time together in the 1990s and early 2000s and were photographed at social events, including with Maxwell and Melania Trump….

Trump, along with others including Clinton, also appeared several times on flight logs for Epstein's private jet.

A 2002 New York magazine profile of Epstein quoted Trump. "I've known Jeff for 15 years. Terrific guy," Trump said. "He's a lot of fun to be with. It is even said that he likes beautiful women as much as I do, and many of them are on the younger side. No doubt about it—Jeffrey enjoys his social life."

Both men said that they subsequently had a falling-out. Trump has said their friendship ended before Epstein pleaded guilty to procuring a minor for prostitution in 2008, served time in a Florida jail and registered as a sex offender….

Maxwell, a British socialite, was convicted in 2021 of helping Epstein's sex-trafficking and sentenced to 20 years in prison. Maxwell didn't respond to a letter requesting an interview sent to her in prison. Arthur Aidala, an attorney who represented Maxwell, said, "At this point, she is focused on her case before the Supreme Court of the United States." …

Epstein's associations with Trump and many powerful people have been well documented….

On September 8, 2025, the WSJ published an article titled "A Visual Breakdown of the Trump Birthday Letter to Epstein" which compares the signature and typeface, drawing style, third-person point of view, and diction in the Letter with prior communications by President Trump (the "September 8 Article"). The September 8 Article includes President Trump's denial that he wrote the Letter or drew the picture and Leavitt's statement in a social media post that President Trump did not draw the picture in or sign the Letter….

President Trump contends that these statements are false because he (1) did not author, sign, or draw any portion of the Letter or direct anyone else to author it; (2) never made or dictated to anyone any of the statements in the voiceover or had any such conversation with Epstein as portrayed in the Letter; and (3) was not "childhood pals" with Epstein….

The court concluded that Trump hadn't actually alleged "actual malice," which is to say knowing or reckless falsehood:

Here, the Amended Complaint falls short of pleading actual malice. Indeed, the allegations regarding malice are conclusory, vague, sometimes inconsistent with the Article, and often irrelevant to whether Defendants knew or should have known that the statements in the Article were purportedly false.

As an initial matter, President Trump's conclusory allegations that Defendants acted with malice because they "knew or should have known" the statements in the Article were false, are insufficient to state a claim. See Reed v. Chamblee (11th Cir. 2025) (finding the plaintiff's conclusory assertions that the defendant acted with actual malice insufficient).

Though vague, the Amended Complaint appears to allege that by choosing to publish the Article despite President Trump's and his team's denials, Defendants acted with actual malice. In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the Letter a "fake," Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story.

But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment. Indeed, were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press—a result that flies in the face of the "American privilege to speak one's mind, although not always with perfect good taste, on all public institutions[.]" Sullivan.

Moreover, the Article did not ignore or minimize President Trump's denial. Rather, it informed readers that President Trump decried the Letter as a fake and denied writing it. By "allowing readers to decide for themselves what to conclude from the [Article], … any allegation of actual malice [is] less plausible." … "[R]eporting perspectives contrary to the publisher's own should be interpreted as helping to rebut, not establish, the presence of actual malice" ….

President Trump's argument that the WSJ Defendants' investigation was inadequate, and therefore an indication of malice, fares no better. As detailed above, a failure to investigate, without more, does not establish actual malice. Rather, "a plaintiff must show the defendant deliberately avoided investigating the veracity of the statement in order to evade learning the truth."

The Amended Complaint comes nowhere close to this standard. Indeed, the Article details a thoughtful and detailed investigation. Before running the story, Defendants contacted President Trump and his team, Justice Department officials, and the FBI for comment.

President Trump and his team responded with his denial, the Justice Department did not respond at all, and the FBI declined to comment. Defendants also attempted to speak with Maxwell; she did not respond to their request and her attorney stated that she was focused on her case before the Supreme Court. In addition, Defendants reached out to other individuals named in the Birthday Book, including Leslie Wexner and Alan Dershowitz, and to individuals involved in binding the Birthday Book, who confirmed that Weitz put the book together. In short, President Trump's allegation that Defendants failed to conduct an adequate investigation is rebutted by the Article and is insufficient to establish actual malice.

{President Trump argues that Harte-Hanks Communications, Inc. v. Connaughton (1989), supports his position that Defendants' purported failure to investigate is enough to support an inference of actual malice. However, in Harte-Hanks, the Supreme Court expressly stated that "[a]lthough failure to investigate will not alone support a finding of actual malice, the purposeful avoidance of the truth is in a different category. Here, President Trump has not alleged any facts, beyond conclusory allegations, that support an inference that Defendants purposefully avoided the truth.}

Grasping at straws, the Amended Complaint attempts to manufacture flaws with the investigation. First, it alleges that the investigation was lacking because Defendants only reviewed the Letter but did not have a copy in their possession. The Court cannot discern any substantive difference—and certainly not one that would establish actual malice—between Defendants reviewing the Letter before publication and obtaining a copy of the Letter. Defendants reviewed the Letter and later reported on its contents. Nothing in the law suggests that Defendants needed to obtain, retain, or publish a copy.

In addition, President Trump's focus on Maxwell is entirely misplaced. The Eleventh Circuit has found "allegations that the Defendants failed to fully investigate their statements by intentionally choosing not to speak with any witnesses who could have refuted the allegedly defamatory statements" insufficient to plead actual malice. And any argument that Defendants "purposely avoided" the truth by either not disclosing what Maxwell told them or by refusing to speak with her is difficult to reconcile with President Trump's own allegations.

The Amended Complaint alleges that "Maxwell has stated, subject to penalty of perjury for lying to a federal officer, that she did not remember President Trump submitting a letter for Epstein's 50th birthday." Based on this allegation, Maxwell had little to offer to Defendants' investigation. In short, references to Maxwell are a red herring and simply do not establish that Defendants "actually entertained serious doubts as to the veracity of the published account[] or was highly aware that the account was probably false."

President Trump's argument that the Article omits certain facts does not save his claims. First, how or why the voiceover in the Letter was typewritten or how the voiceover was confirmed to be in the third person are inconsequential details that have no bearing on whether Defendants published the Article knowing its contents were false or with reckless disregard as to its falsity. Moreover, Defendants' decisions about how to investigate and what to include in the Article do not establish malice. "Obviously the author of an article will have to choose which facts to include and which to omit. It is impossible to print all of the facts on which an opinion or belief is based …. Were the courts or criticized [parties] to be allowed to dictate the contents of such articles, censorship would have won out over free speech and the right to dissent."

Finally, the allegation that Defendants intentionally omitted President Trump's denial that he signed the Letter or a discussion on whether the signature on the Letter is authentic, is belied by the Article. It states, multiple times, that President Trump denies writing the Letter and that "[i]t isn't clear how the letter with Trump's signature was prepared." . This is more than sufficient to encompass any denial that he "signed" the Letter or that the signature on the Letter is authentic.

The Amended Complaint's reliance on the September 8 Article to establish malice is equally unavailing. Nothing in the law suggests that a journalist must report on every piece of evidence they uncover before going to print. Moreover, it is unclear why President Trump argues the September 8 Article shows that his signature "could not be more different" than the one in the Letter, when it contains several examples where President Trump's actual signature and sketches are similar to those in the Letter. At bottom, the September 8 Article does not support a finding that Defendants knew or should have known that President Trump did not sign the Letter….

#7566. The Debanking Scandal Started in Washington, Not Wall Street

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has confirmed what conservatives have said for years. The OCC's 47-page report, released Wednesday after reviewing 100,000 complaints and 50,000 internal bank records, found that between 2020 and 2025 the nation’s nine largest national banks denied service to Americans because of their political, social, or religious beliefs.

The details are ugly. JPMorgan’s WePay payment unit closed the account of a merchant selling “MAGA” themed merchandise, and its screening system flagged phrases like “America First.” It shut down a religious non-profit because the Southern Poverty Law Center, since indicted on federal fraud charges, had branded it a hate group.

PNC refused a line of credit to a media company because one owner’s foundation had funded Christian conservative groups. Banks also choked off financing to entire lawful industries like firearms, coal, Arctic oil and gas, private prisons, tobacco, etc. While the instinct is to blame the banks, a different culprit emerges in the report’s details.

Banks feared negative press, protests, and organized activist criticism. But the greatest fear was reprisals from regulators and politicians, because those can actually shut down a financial institution.

>>> Regions Financial’s Reasonable Retreat From Ideology

A Wells Fargo review of a prospective firearms client was blunt: under the Biden administration, banks could face “greater supervisory pressure to move away from lending to the firearms industry.” Another bank dropped private-prison clients citing “changing policymaker attitudes,” then tried to win one back just months into the Trump administration. 

Those aren’t the actions of institutions pursuing an ideological crusade but of businesses reading the weather in Washington. That’s the real scandal in the OCC report.

Banks don’t operate in a free market so much as under the permanent supervision of federal examiners who can downgrade their ratings, initiate expensive investigations, and impose costly enforcement actions.

For years, those examiners graded banks on “reputational risk,” a category with no financial definition or objective yardstick. While a loan defaulting is a pass-or-fail course, reputational risk is whatever a regulator wants it to be, with no financial impact required.

A deposit account for a pro-life ministry poses no inherent danger to a bank’s balance sheet. Neither does a loan to a firearms manufacturer or payment services for a conservative think tank. But when the regulators who effectively control your fate hate those groups, a threatening phone call from the government can result in debanking.

That’s how faceless bureaucrats circumnavigate the Constitution. Officials who could never lawfully seize a disfavored group’s money can simply make it costly for banks to hold it. The Supreme Court unanimously rejected that tactic in NRA v. Vullo in 2024, holding that regulators may not coerce the firms they oversee into punishing protected speech. Yet the practice persisted, because it rarely leaves fingerprints.

For those who believe in free markets and individual liberty, debanking was doubly offensive because it wasn’t a market failure but a regulatory distortion. Left to sound financial judgment, banks have every reason to serve profitable, lawful customers. It took government pressure to make turning away business look like the safe choice.

Fortunately, the Trump administration has acted. Its August 2025 executive order directed regulators to end politicized debanking, and the OCC has stopped using reputational risk in examinations. But executive orders and agency guidance can be reversed on the first day of the next administration. Another far-left White House could revive reputational risk, restore the quiet phone calls, and start the cycle over.

>>> Elizabeth Warren’s Big Government Power Grab Will Make Depositors Pay

Congress ought to step up and make that impossible by enshrining into law protections for bank customers and the banks themselves so that the latter cannot be unconstitutionally coerced by regulators. Federal law should prohibit non-financial and nonsensical metrics like reputational risk from supervision and forbid officials from pressuring institutions to drop lawful customers without a documented, quantifiable financial reason.

Rules like that don’t expand government but restrain it, keeping regulators focused on safety and soundness, not their private political preferences.

Furthermore, whatever standards must apply evenly. Fintechs, payment processors, and other non-bank firms are increasingly providing the deposit and payment services Americans use every day. It’s no accident that WePay, a payment platform, produced some of the report’s worst examples.

If those firms are exempt, politicized gatekeeping just migrates to the less-regulated, and fast-growing, corner of the market. Firms offering the same services must play by the same rules.

Americans should never have to wonder whether their bank account depends on their politics. The debanking pressure came from Washington, and the fix has to come from Washington too, written into law where the next administration can’t quietly undo it.

#7565. The Greenland Deal Is a Huge Success

Ignore the naysayers: President Trump’s successful conclusion of the Greenland deal with the governments of Denmark and Greenland is a huge win for the United States, and also one that will improve Danish, Greenlandic and, indeed, trans-Atlantic security.

This is a major diplomatic achievement. It expands U.S. defense areas in Greenland, prohibits a non-NATO military presence, and protects critical parts of the Greenlandic economy that adversarial governments could otherwise use for dual-use purposes.

The agreement contains language clarifying the core U.S. interests at stake and the rationale behind increasing activities in the Arctic, recognizing “the security challenges in the Arctic and the High North posed by adversaries’ increased military activity and growing strategic interest in the region” and that “the security situation in the Arctic is changing and that more efforts are needed to ensure security there in the future.”

Critics have said the deal is the same as the one we had before. Not true. The 2026 agreement augments, updates and improves the 1951 treaty, expanding U.S. military infrastructure on the island with two new bases at Narsarsuaq and Mestersvig. It also prohibits Russian or Chinese military bases in Greenland, and creates a mechanism for the governments in Copenhagen, Nuuk and Washington to veto investment in critical parts of the Greenlandic economy. Importantly, the new agreement and its provisions will continue to apply even if Greenland becomes independent.

The strategic rationale for the United States to maintain a military presence in Greenland and secure it from adversarial influence should be obvious. Greenland commands the approaches to the North Atlantic and North America, forming the northwestern end of the Greenland-Iceland-U.K. (GIUK) Gap through which Russian ships and submarines entering the North Atlantic pass. At more than 836,000 square miles, Greenland is a major geographic shaper of the Arctic region, and U.S. radars based in Greenland play an essential role in detecting and intercepting any hostile movements toward the U.S. mainland.

>>> Why America Should Take the Lead in Greenland—Before Our Adversaries Do

Indeed, the strategic rationale for American military presence in Greenland is strongest when considered in the context of great power competition. The Arctic is the shortest and most likely path for strategic bombers or intercontinental ballistic missiles heading toward the United States, and Greenland in particular lies in the shortest and most likely path for these systems when fired from Russia. Pituffik Space Base, an existing U.S. military site in Greenland, supports American missile warning, missile defense and space surveillance.

Greenland is an autonomous territory of the Kingdom of Denmark, with significant self-rule but responsibility for defense resting with the Danish government in Copenhagen. Russia and China have consistently demonstrated interest in the island and surrounding region, with Chinese investments in particular targeting Greenland’s key economic sectors and infrastructure.

To combat this, the deal also creates a mechanism for the three parties to deny Chinese or Russian investment in key Greenlandic sectors such as ports, airports and mines. Greenland is estimated to possess 1.5 million tons of critical mineral reserves. Denmark had already played a positive role in preventing malign investment in critical sectors of the Greenlandic economy, but the new deal formalizes the need and mechanism for doing this and gives the United States a say.

>>> How Norway Can Do More To Forestall the Russian Threat

Denmark has long been a very strong and reliable ally of the United States. Danish troops served in combat roles alongside Americans in Afghanistan after the 9/11 attacks and suffered one of the highest casualty rates in the war among our NATO allies. Denmark is one of the highest spenders on defense within the NATO alliance, had already reached 3.2 percent of gross domestic product as of 2025, and is projected to reach the mandated 3.5 percent spending level in the near future — among the first NATO allies to do so.

Much of Denmark’s new spending is going into capabilities relevant to defending its Arctic territory. The successful conclusion of this agreement, of course, will create new avenues for Arctic security cooperation between the American and Danish militaries.

The American, Danish and Greenlandic peoples have a shared interest in a secure Arctic where Russia is unable to threaten North America or Europe and where China (a non-Arctic state) is unable to meddle where it doesn’t belong.

This deal secures the sovereign security and economic interests of Washington, Copenhagen, and Nuuk and helps cement trans-Atlantic security cooperation in the Arctic for decades to come.

#7564. Sir Patrick Stewart, RIP

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Stewart's portrayal of Captain Jean Luc Picard was a great achievement, and epitomized the values of Star Trek.

The great British actor Sir Patrick Stewart passed away on Thursday. While Stewart began his career as a stage actor and performed in many Shakespeare plays, he is best known for his portrayal of Captain Jean-Luc Picard, in Star Trek: The Next Generation. Thanks to his impressive performance, Stewart and the character he played became science fiction icons.

Stewart brought extraordinary depth and perception to the role. And the character is an interesting contrast to the more instinctive and aggressive, less cerebral, Captain Kirk in the original Star Trek Series. Perhaps more than any other character, Stewart's Picard epitomized Star Trek's progressive liberal values: Enlightenment rationalism, technological optimism (highlighted by his defense of the rights of the android Data), racial and ethnic equality, and commitment to peace and diplomacy.

In many ways, Picard and TNG promoted these ideas to an even greater extent than the original series. Whereas Captain Kirk was often belligerent and acted on instinct, Picard sought diplomatic solutions to conflict, and tried to avoid doing anything drastic without careful deliberation. In the original series, the Klingons and Romulans are mostly depicted as evil and irreconcilable enemies of the Federation, in TNG the Klingons have become allies and there is hope that there will be peace with the Romulans, as well. In multiple episodes, Picard takes the lead in working to maintain and improve Federation relations with these and other previously hostile alien societies.

There is much to admire in this ideology and Picard's advocacy of it. But, as I have pointed out in a 2016 article (see also this more recent piece), Star Trek's ideology has a dark side, as well: its uncritical embrace of socialism. This is also reflected in the Federation's seeming ideological homogeneity. Picard also exemplifies this negative aspect of Star Trek ideology, with his thinly veiled disdain for private enterprise, and people who seek to make a profit.

As depicted by Stewart, the Picard character also highlights another key tension in Star Trek ideology, this one relating to cultural diversity. Picard is supposed to be French; but other than his noticeable British accent, he seems little different from other human Federation characters. The "Doylist" real-world explanation for this is that Stewart himself was British, and trying to get him to speak with a French accent might have had bad results. But the "Watsonian" in-universe effect of this is to accentuate how the human characters in Star Trek have largely lost their cultural distinctiveness. French, British, and other human cultures have largely blended together, by the 24th century (when the show is set). Star Trek may champion diversity. But, culturally and politically, the human characters are mostly people who look different, but largely think alike on almost all major issues. The few dissenters are generally depicted as either villains or fools.

As  I have previously noted, this ideological homogeneity and uncritical acceptance of Federation ideology gets challenged more in later Star Trek series, beginning with Deep Space 9. DS-9 and later series depict more ideological conflict among humans, and raise serious questions about Federation ideology. But Stewart's Picard remains an iconic depiction of Federation ideals.

As always in assessing actors, we should not assume that the character necessarily reflects the views of the actor. We can and should recognize Picard's shortcomings and those of Federation ideology, without blaming Stewart for them. Indeed, his performance deserves credit for providing a valuable window into these issues.

The more recent Picard series is not as good as TNG. But I would argue the blame for that rests with the producers and their problematic plotlines, rather than Stewart.

In addition to his justly famous Star Trek role, Stewart also starred in the X-Men movie series (which I won't comment on, as I know little about it). His first significant science fiction role was playing Gurney Halleck in the 1984 movie version of Dune.

The 1984 Dune movie is an incoherent mess, and not as good as the more recent Denis Villeneuve version (see my reviews of the latter here and here). But Stewart did a great job with his role, and really brought Halleck to life.

In sum, Sir Patrick Stewart was a great actor, and well deserves his status as an SF icon. He will be greatly missed.

UPDATE: The original version of this post had the date of Patrick Stewart's death wrong (off by one day). I apologize for the mistake, which has now been corrected.

#7563. Corporate Alignment with the Human Rights Campaign: Legal, Financial, and Reputational Risks for Shareholders

In 2024, Bowyer Research conducted two coordinated shareholder engagement campaigns targeting more than 400 publicly traded U.S. companies, focusing on potential risks related to corporate alignment with the Human Rights Campaign (HRC)—particularly through participation in the HRC’s Corporate Equality Index (CEI)—and from extensive Pride Month messaging. This Backgrounder summarizes the substance and scale of those engagements and documents the legal, financial, reputational, and moral concerns raised by shareholders, with particular attention to policies and communications involving children.

The Corporate Equality Index has served as the primary mechanism through which the HRC exerts its influence on corporate governance, employment policy, and public messaging. Participation is nominally voluntary, but companies that achieve a perfect score of 100 are required to satisfy a set of criteria that, because it is ever-evolving and regularly expanded, creates more and more compliance obligations with no defined endpoint. These criteria now include coverage of sex-rejecting procedures for minors as employee health benefits, mandatory identity-based training programs, and public corporate endorsement of contested social positions.[REF]

Shareholders represented by Bowyer Research, most notably The Heritage Foundation, engaged these companies to identify legal vulnerabilities, financial risks, and the structural incompatibility of CEI participation with sound, long-term fiduciary governance.

The Corporate Equality Index: Structure and Escalating Demands

The Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index is a benchmarking tool that scores corporations on their compliance with a defined set of employment, benefits, and public-messaging criteria. First introduced in 2002, the CEI has expanded steadily in scope, and its criteria are revised fairly frequently.

Bowyer Research’s engagement database, compiled in collaboration with the 1792 Exchange, focused on 160 companies that publicly promote perfect CEI scores of 100. These companies span a variety of sectors, including technology, finance, health care, retail, energy, and consumer goods, and reflect the broad reach of the HRC’s influence across America’s capital markets.[REF]

Companies frequently present perfect CEI scores as evidence of commendable corporate citizenship, but shareholders represented by Bowyer Research take a contrary view: A score of 100 is evidence not of sound governance, but rather of deep structural entanglement with a controversial external activist organization’s ideological compliance demands. Because the HRC revises its criteria frequently, companies committed to maintaining a perfect score face escalating requirements with no defined endpoint. This process is incompatible with sensible risk management and long-term shareholder value creation.

More to the point, current CEI requirements extend well beyond foundational anti-discrimination policies. They include or have included, among other criteria, employee health benefit coverage for sex-rejecting transition procedures (including for minor dependents); mandatory participation in identity-based employee training programs (prior to this year); and a demonstrated pattern of “outreach” to the LGBTQ community, often involving support for contested social and political positions. Each of these creates distinct legal, financial, and reputational risks.

Legal and Regulatory Exposure

CEI participation creates legal vulnerability across several distinct areas of law. The 1792 Exchange has documented these risks in its Corporate Bias Ratings analysis, noting that the CEI “promotes policies that may violate existing civil rights laws” and that participation exposes companies to “unnecessary legal risks.”[REF]

  • Employment Discrimination. Policies that prioritize gender identity over biological sex in employment have generated litigation under the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and similar state statutes. The case of Activision illustrates how these policies can generate claims from multiple directions simultaneously—from allegations of discriminatory treatment on the basis of gender identity to allegations of discrimination arising from the company’s CEI policies that infringe on the well-grounded rights of others.[REF]
  • Religious Discrimination. Mandatory participation in gender-affirming or identity-based training programs has produced religious discrimination claims in federal courts. A lawsuit involving Alaska Airlines, in which employees alleged that mandatory diversity training conflicted with sincerely held religious beliefs, illustrates the risk companies face when compliance with external advocacy frameworks meets statutory protections for religious belief.[REF]
  • State-Level Legislative Risk. Benefits policies that include coverage for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones, and irreversible sex-rejecting surgical procedures for minor dependents are increasingly subject to state restrictions. As more states limit or prohibit procedures for minors—including treating such procedures as child abuse[REF]—companies that include them as standard employee health benefits may find themselves in conflict with state law, creating complex compliance obligations and potential liability exposure.[REF]

Financial and Brand Risk: Lessons from High-Profile Cases

The financial consequences of activist-aligned corporate messaging are notably well documented. Several high-profile cases provide clear evidence of material harm to shareholders.

  • Bud Light. Anheuser-Busch InBev's 2023 promotional partnership with transgender social media influencer Dylan Mulvaney resulted in a consumer boycott that produced an estimated $1 billion or more in lost sales and a sustained, multi-quarter decline in Bud Light’s market share, dropping from the number-one brand overall to number three.[REF]
  • Target. Target Corporation’s introduction of a controversial Pride merchandise collection that included “tuck-friendly” swimsuits in 2023 generated significant consumer backlash that had a measurable adverse impact on the company’s revenues and share price. Target scaled back its 2024 Pride Month campaign significantly—a widely noted signal that even companies with historically strong activist-alignment track records need to be open to reassessing risks.[REF]
  • Disney. Disney’s public positioning against Florida’s Parental Rights in Education legislation resulted in the loss of the company’s Reedy Creek special tax district, significant negative media coverage, and a period of brand and financial turbulence.[REF] The episode demonstrated that corporate activism on politically contested issues can result in unwanted regulatory and legislative attention.

These cases illustrate a consistent pattern: Activist-aligned corporate messaging that extends beyond non-discrimination into overt participation in polarized cultural debates creates consumer division, brand damage, and measurable financial losses. The 1792 Exchange’s analysis concludes that such alignment “divides employees, alienates customers, and distracts businesses from making good products and services.”[REF]

Child-Related Concerns: Medical, Moral, and Reputational Dimensions

A central and especially sensitive element of both engagement campaigns involved corporate policies and messaging that affect or appear to target children. Shareholders characterized this domain as a moral and reputational red line—one with consequences that extend well beyond standard brand-risk frameworks.

  • Health Benefits for Minors. The CEI’s rating criteria encourage or require companies to include coverage for puberty blockers, sterilizing cross-sex hormones, and sex-rejecting surgeries for minor dependents as part of standard employee benefits packages.[REF] State-level restrictions create growing compliance complexity. Additionally, studies on the long-term medical effects of puberty suppression and cross-sex hormone administration on minors have shown that the risks and harms substantially outweigh any known benefits. In fact, several American and European health authorities have recently restricted such interventions pending further evidence.[REF] Offering benefits that facilitate irreversible medical procedures for minors creates significant exposure with a substantial segment of the consumer population.
  • Marketing and Messaging Involving Children. Pride Month engagement placed particular emphasis on the intersection of sexualized content and children in corporate marketing, in-store displays, and digital communications. Consumer research consistently demonstrates that parents are highly protective of their children, as a result of which they desire to prevent their exposure to sexualized content, and that brands perceived as targeting children with such messaging suffer long-term reputational harm.

Coerced Speech, Workplace Risk, and Employee Relations

Beyond benefits and public-facing messaging, the Bowyer/Heritage engagement campaigns addressed the internal workplace implications of HRC-driven compliance frameworks. Three categories of concern were identified.

  • Compelled Expression of Ideological Positions. Requiring employees to display ideological symbols such as pride flags or related insignia on uniforms or company-affiliated digital profiles constitutes compelled speech. This practice raises both moral and potential legal concerns and risks alienating employees who have sincere scientific, ethical, and religious beliefs that differ from the positions they are required to endorse.
  • Mandatory Identity-Based Training (prior to 2026). Unconscious bias and privilege-acknowledgment training programs that require employees to segregate or make affirmations based on race, sex, or gender identity create both discrimination exposure and workforce morale risks. As documented above, mandatory participation in such programs has already produced federal litigation.
  • Selective Inclusion Policies. Genuine inclusion requires protection for all employees, including those whose views differ from those of activist organizations. Companies that apply inclusion principles selectively risk discrimination claims and undermine the internal cohesion that drives long-term organizational success. The CEI’s “Responsible Citizenship” rating criterion penalizes companies up to 25 points for irresponsible citizenship, including donating to “anti-LGBT” non-religious groups.[REF]

The Scale and Scope of Shareholder Concern

The scope of the Bowyer Research/Heritage Foundation 2024 engagement efforts reflects the breadth of shareholder concern about these issues.[REF]

The CEI-focused engagement letter was distributed to 160 corporate contacts spanning technology, finance, health care, retail, energy, and consumer goods.[REF] Recipients included Amazon, Disney, Coca-Cola, PepsiCo, Johnson & Johnson, McDonald’s, Bank of America, BlackRock, Visa, Mastercard, Microsoft, and many others, demonstrating that shareholder concern about HRC influence is far-reaching and distributed broadly across the U.S. economy.

Pride Month messaging engagement was distributed to nearly 400 companies.[REF] In both engagement campaigns, shareholders communicated that they hold sufficient share positions to qualify to submit a proxy resolution at the next annual meeting but also expressed a preference for constructive direct dialogue before resorting to formal shareholder mechanisms.

A Gallup survey cited in the engagement materials found that a majority of U.S. adults do not want companies to speak publicly on political and social issues—confirming that the concerns raised by these shareholders reflect a significant segment of the consumer and investor base.[REF]

Recommendations for Action

Based on the evidence developed in the Bowyer Research/Heritage Foundation engagement campaigns as outlined in this analysis, it is recommended that corporate boards, investors, and policymakers seriously consider the following specific actions.

  • End or limit CEI participation. Participation in the CEI by Fortune 500 companies has declined by 65 percent in 2026. This serves as evidence that efforts to eliminate overt politicization of corporations can have a significant impact. The boards of corporations that maintain their participation in the HRC’s Corporate Equality Index should evaluate whether ongoing participation serves the long-term interests of shareholders, employees, and customers. Given the continually escalating nature of CEI requirements and their attendant, documented legal and reputational risks, companies should conduct a structured risk review before seeking renewal of participation or actions that would result in a “perfect score.”
  • Review benefits policies affecting minors. Companies should conduct a thorough legal and risk review of health benefit policies that include coverage for sex-rejecting procedures or treatments for minor dependents, accounting for evolving state law, current medical evidence, and potential litigation exposure. It should be noted in this connection that on October 22, 2025, the United States District Court for the Southern District of Mississippi issued an order vacating provisions of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services’ “Nondiscrimination in Health Programs and Activities” final rule relating to gender-identity discrimination. Consequently, the provision of health coverage for sex-rejecting procedures is no longer required under Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act.[REF]
  • End sponsorship of the Human Rights Campaign and the HRC Foundation.[REF] Companies should limit sponsorships and partnerships to organizations that advance the interests of shareholders. Sponsorships and partnerships that are not business-related draw unnecessary scrutiny to the company and waste shareholder resources.
  • Limit public communications to core business. Companies should resist external pressure to engage in overt cultural advocacy and focus public communications instead on products, services, and business performance. In other words, businesses should focus on business.
  • Adopt viewpoint-neutral inclusion frameworks. Rather than pursuing scores on advocacy-affiliated benchmarks, companies should adopt more viewpoint-neutral inclusion frameworks—such as the Alliance Defending Freedom’s Viewpoint Diversity Score—that protect all employees regardless of their political, cultural, or religious perspectives.[REF]
  • Establish explicit protections for content that involves children. Companies should adopt clear policies prohibiting sexualized imagery or messaging in connection with children in marketing, in-store displays, or digital communications.
  • Ensure voluntary participation in training programs. Companies should review mandatory training programs for potential legal exposure under civil rights and religious freedom statutes and ensure that no employee is segregated or required to make affirmations that conflict with his or her sincerely held beliefs.

Conclusion

Corporate alignment with the Human Rights Campaign—particularly through participation in the Corporate Equality Index—creates a set of escalating legal, financial, reputational, and moral risks that fiduciary-minded companies can no longer treat as cost-free. The evidence from Bud Light, Target, and Disney demonstrates that activist-aligned messaging often leads to real financial harm. The structure of the CEI ensures that today’s compliance threshold becomes tomorrow’s minimum with no natural endpoint.

The concerns raised in the Bowyer Research/Heritage Foundation 2024 engagement campaigns—spanning more than 400 publicly traded companies—are backed by logic and evidence. They reflect the views of a broad and growing segment of the investor community and are supported by legal precedent, consumer research, and cautionary lessons from companies that have already paid a significant price for over-alignment with external activist agendas.

Corporate boards have both the authority and the fiduciary obligation to evaluate these risks clearly. Genuine inclusion—of all employees, customers, and shareholders—requires resistance to selective ideological capture, not capitulation to it. Companies that refocus on core business performance, protect employees of all viewpoints, and resist activist pressure will be better positioned to deliver long-term value to the shareholders they serve.

Stephen R. Soukup is a Visiting Fellow in the Free Enterprise Initiative at The Heritage Foundation. Jerry Bowyer is CEO of Bowyer Research, a proxy voting and corporate engagement consulting firm specializing in shareholder advocacy on issues of corporate governance, risk management, and fiduciary responsibility.

Appendix A: CEI Shareholder Engagement Letter

The following is the verbatim text of the engagement letter distributed to 160 companies regarding their participation in the Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index.

Bowyer Research is a proxy voting and corporate engagement consulting firm. Our clients, who are your shareholders, are extremely concerned about the company embroiling itself in non-core business advocacy of some of the most divisive issues in American life. A prime example would be the Human Rights Campaign’s Corporate Equality Index. Our data indicates that you participate in this survey and have a score of 100. It is important that you understand that for many shareholders, a 100 is not an A plus, it is an F minus, especially when some of the specific demands of the HRC are factored in, such as paying for puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and (irreversible) surgeries for minors as a health benefit.

We represent X investors who hold Y shares in COMPANY.

It is always our preference to begin with a request for dialogue before moving ahead with shareholder proposals.

We share the concerns of the 1792 Exchange, whose analysis of the CEI and its risks is as follows:

Participation in the Human Rights Campaign’s (HRC) Corporate Equality Index (CEI) exposes corporations to unnecessary legal risks by promoting policies that may violate existing civil rights laws. For example, the CEI encourages companies to adopt controversial stances on gender identity, which can lead to litigation under the Civil Rights Act of 1964 and similar state laws. For instance, prioritizing gender identity over biological sex in employment practices has led to discrimination lawsuits, as seen with Activision. Additionally, mandating employees to attend gender-affirming training could result in religious discrimination claims, as evidenced by the lawsuit involving Alaska Airlines. Furthermore, companies open themselves up to financial risks and brand harm by adopting the policies of the CEI. High-profile cases, such as Bud Light’s collaboration with a transgender activist and Target’s controversial ‘Pride’ collection, resulted in consumer boycotts that led to financial losses of billions of dollars. Aligning with the CEI divides employees, alienates customers, and distracts businesses from making good products and services. Prioritizing shareholder interests and consumer satisfaction over the demands of radical activist groups is a better path to long-term success.

You can view the 1792 Exchange’s evaluation of your company in their Corporate Bias Ratings database (https://1792exchange.com/spotlight-reports/corporate-bias-ratings). We note that under the influence of journalist Robby Starbuck, many companies have been, wisely, rethinking their relationship with the Human Rights Campaign. If a company participates in HRC’s survey but not in surveys such as the Alliance Defending Freedom’s viewpoint-neutral Viewpoint Diversity Survey, we are well justified in thinking of that company as taking sides in a culture war with shareholders’ dollars.

Appendix B: Pride Month Shareholder Engagement Letter

The following is the verbatim text of the engagement letter distributed to approximately 400 companies regarding Pride Month messaging practices.

We know that you are under constant pressure from outside activist groups and well-organized subsectors of your employees to go full-in this June on Pride Month. We urge you to remember that they do not represent the voices of everyone. Many of your shareholders, including the ones we represent, are concerned that June messaging goes beyond the commonsense acknowledgement that all customers and employees should be treated equally and with dignity and tips into taking sides in a deeply polarizing culture war. We think you want to avoid this, and we want you to know that we will back you when you do.

We see Disney, Target and Bud Light as cautionary tales of ways in which companies have been cajoled into brand-destructive messaging. We note that even Target is pulling back this year. That should speak volumes to those who have ears to hear.

We especially want the company to be aware of the extreme sensitivity that the majority of your customers have regarding the mixing of highly sexualized content and minors. Parents are naturally highly protective of their children and do not want them targeted with sexual messaging. This is a red line, morally and reputationally. Don’t cross it. Customers have long memories where kids are concerned.

We also urge you not to force sexual identity flair and paraphernalia onto the uniforms of service employees, nor onto their business-related websites. Coerced speech is morally unjustifiable and legally actionable. If an employee doesn’t want to be forced to fly the rainbow flag, they should not be forced to.

The same is true for ‘unconscious bias training’ sessions in which employees are forced to confess to various privileges inherent in having a sexual identity that is not among the current ideologically protected classes. You should let every employee bring their whole self to work, and employees who are not ‘allies’ should have their viewpoints protected against discrimination.

Of course, employees should be evaluated based solely on merit. LGBTQ employees should not be discriminated against, but neither should employees who dissent from the political or cultural views of that interest group. Inclusion is for everybody, otherwise it isn’t inclusion at all—it’s just taking sides. And it is not in your or your shareholders’ interests for the company to be taking sides.

A slim majority of Americans do not want companies speaking publicly on political and social issues (Gallup, 2024). The shareholders we represent possess sufficient shares to easily qualify to propose resolutions for the proxy statement of the next annual meeting, but we believe the proposal system is a fallback for companies that are not responsive to shareholder concerns, not a first resort. We hope this is something you are willing to genuinely discuss.

#7562. Trump Won’t Betray Britain Over the Falklands

In his second term, Donald Trump has aggressively pursued an America First foreign policy. And rightly so. The U.S. president represents the American people, and every policy he advances should be in his nation’s interest. But backing British sovereignty over the Falkland Islands fits firmly within this vision, and his administration should stand shoulder to shoulder with the UK on an issue of huge importance to the British people.

Last month, in response to questions from British media, President Trump declared that the U.S. would review its long-standing policy of neutrality on the Falklands issue. This was immediately seized upon by Argentina’s president Javier Milei, a close ally of Trump, who announced tougher sanctions against foreign companies with plans to drill for oil around the Falkland Islands, as well as a renewed push to end British sovereignty.

The U.S. president has also seemed to equivocate over the question of whether the U.S. would come to Britain’s aid in the event of a future war between London and Buenos Aires. Trump made it clear he was hugely disappointed in the refusal of the British Government to back U.S. military action against Iran.

>>> Trump Will Never Forgive Burnham if the Chagos Deal Is Resurrected

Having worked closely with the U.S. administration in opposition to Labour’s disastrous Chagos surrender deal, I have witnessed first-hand the White House’s immense frustration with Britain’s socialist government, which has frequently been at odds with Trump’s team, from the Iran war and Israel to net zero, mass migration and freedom of speech. The Trump administration has been particularly unhappy over Labour dragging its feet on a firm commitment to swiftly increase defence spending in line with Nato commitments made at the Hague summit last year.

This is the tensest relationship that I have seen between London and Washington in nearly a quarter of a century in the D.C. policy world. The reality is that Labour simply isn’t trusted, and the renewed push on Chagos by No 10 under Andy Burnham on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly further underscored this. The British Government has been acting as its own worst enemy.

But I do not believe the Trump presidency will ultimately shift the U.S. position on the Falklands, despite all the stupid actions of the Labour Government. Here’s why.

The Anglo-American special relationship still matters inside the Washington Beltway, in both the executive branch and on Capitol Hill. The King’s visit to the U.S. in April was a stunning success, with even “No Kings” Democrat Members of Congress giving King Charles a series of standing ovations when he spoke to a joint session of Congress.

President Trump’s extremely warm reception for the King at the White House and his speech welcoming the King at the arrival ceremony, which I attended, were a glowing tribute to the enduring strength of our two great nations. The bottom line is that President Trump loves Britain, the British people and his British heritage through his Scottish mother. And like Trump, nearly 60 million Americans have British ancestry according to the 2020 census, including much of America’s political and economic leadership.

>>> How the U.S.-Europe Rift Got Balkanized

Throw into the mix the massive levels of trade and investment between the two countries, the vital strategic importance of the U.S./UK base at Diego Garcia, the key role played by RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire (despite the decision to temporarily remove U.S. stealth strategic bombers in the wake of an Iranian terror plot), and the extremely close intelligence ties between the CIA and MI6, and the special relationship remains very real.

Not a single American official I have spoken with in the last few months has told me they support a change in U.S. policy over the Falklands. They understand the huge importance this issue has to the British people, and all of them speak of their admiration for Margaret Thatcher who ordered the liberation of the islands from Argentina following the brutal invasion by its military junta in 1982.

U.S. officials also acknowledge that the Argentine position over the Falklands was viewed sympathetically by the Obama administration when Hillary Clinton was Secretary of State and far-Left Cristina Kirchner was Argentina’s president. Republicans are reluctant to take a stance that Democrats have traditionally favored in Washington, and which would be championed by the American Left.

There remains immense goodwill in the United States towards Great Britain and the British people, and very little desire to throw America’s closest ally under the bus over the Falklands. It is firmly in the U.S. national interest to defend the vital principles of sovereignty and self-determination the American people cherish.

#7560. Ignition, Inc.: MSP Mac Help Desk Guru (work from home)

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

The tech you'll work with (and grow into)

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Yes, PCs too — about one-third of our users are driving Windows

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 admin consoles

Identity and access — SSO, MFA, and security keys (Okta, Entra ID, Yubikey, and friends)

Lots of other security tools — our stack is constantly evolving and may vary from client to client

The everyday productivity stack — Slack, Zoom, conference-room AV, networking basics (Meraki), and endpoint tooling

⠀ You don't need to know all of this. You need to be the kind of person who wants to. As you grow, there's a clear path into infrastructure administration, project architecture and implementation, and — for the right person — security and compliance work (phishing simulations, endpoint detection, SOC 2 / CIS / SEC readiness, due diligence questionnaire support, etc.). That's where our most senior people live, and it's wide open.

The hard requirements — we won't move forward unless you:

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Have a quiet home workspace and reliable broadband

Have proven Apple aptitude — you actually use and like the Apple ecosystem

Have at least 5 years of IT support experience on the job.

⠀ Everything else — and this is the longer list, on purpose. We figure technical skills are teachable; character takes a lot longer. So we're looking for someone who:

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. If you’re an AI tinkerer, great! We want to hear how you’re using it and see your latest vibe project. If you’re allergic to AI or have no interest in learning new habits to work effectively with it, this is not the place for you.

Base salary: Applicants outside the USA will be compensated according to your local employment market. For applicants closer to the junior side who are located in the USA, $50,000–$65,000/yr, depending on experience level and your local geographical price index. With experience, comp goes up from there. Genuinely experienced, more senior candidates can be slotted higher — let's talk.

Type & location: Full-time, work from home, fully remote. Eastern or Pacific time zones.

Benefits: Medical / dental / vision for the employee, 401(k) with employer contribution, 2 weeks of PTO annually to start, and a stipend for your home internet.

The first step is really easy and only takes 10 minutes — no resume, no cover letter, no essays. Here's how:

Take this online Culture Index assessment (about 10 minutes): We use it to screen for people whose natural wiring fits how our team works.

If your profile lines up with what we're looking for, we'll reach out and ask you to complete a 60-minute TestGorilla assessment for critical thinking skills, send us your resume, and maybe a couple of other items.

From there, we conduct between 2-4 video interviews. One of these might be a live technical assessment.

If the Culture Index step feels like a strange way to start a job application — that's kind of the point. Remember the phrase Think Different?

Ignition is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome and will consider all qualified applicants. Good luck in your search — and may the Force be with you!

No forms. Just smart, optimized applications.

Write cover letters and job applications just by speaking.

#7559. France Is Learning the Hard Way What Happens When the Socialist Bill Comes Due

“Is Paris Burning?”

The title of that 1960s movie came from a message Adolf Hitler sent to his commanding general in Paris in August 1944. He wanted Paris to burn if he couldn’t keep it.

Today, the call isn’t coming from the Führerbunker; it’s from inside the house. It’s not Nazis, but the French—and quasi-French—burning Paris and other French cities.

The Louvre museum in Paris, home to the Mona Lisa, closed Monday “due to a student social movement.” That’s one way to describe the utter chaos overtaking French cities.

In Limoges, rioters set fire to the town hall, destroying its iconic tower. In Marseille, they broke into city hall and vandalized the interior. In Paris, a video circulating online appeared to show young thugs shouting, “Wallah! Kill her!” and “Dirty whore!” [my translation] at a policewoman they chased and threw to the ground—all while trashing property and assaulting people on the streets.

>>> France’s Education Collapse Is a Warning for America

What’s happening in France is both familiar and new. It’s familiar in that mass protests are endemic to France. They happen every few years when a feckless government tries to balance the books by reforming France’s ruinously generous public benefits. What’s new is the addition of foreign influence and the scale of the violence.

The high-schoolers who kicked off this round of protests are angry about class sizes, dilapidated schools, and access to college. Retirees who joined them say state pensions aren’t enough to live on. Everyone complains about the high cost of living. They all want more state spending to cure their ills.

French protests often turn violent. Torched cars, vandalized property, and looting are common. What has added fuel to the fire this time is the “Casseurs” (breakers), looters, and violent thugs going beyond what was tacitly tolerated in the past. Many seem to be of migrant background, and some carry Palestinian flags or those of the North African countries they or their parents came from.

Videos in French media showed streets of looted stores. Rue Paradis in Marseille has many high-end jewelry and fashion stores, but also many mom-and-pop shops whose owners work long hours for little profit. Dozens of these are now looted shells. Their metal shutters—designed to prevent windows from being broken and stores from being burglarized—lie torn off or broken.

Many of France’s major cities are run by socialists. Marseille’s mayor, Benoit Payan, blames the French government for failing to protect city hall—where his own office is—and local stores. He wants Paris to pay for all the damage. Once again, the French taxpayer is on the hook.

How does this end? Not quickly. The political left is well organized, galvanized, and funded—including with foreign money. We are likely to see more promises of increased spending from lame-duck President Emmanuel Macron, now in the last year of his two terms and unable to run again. He gave a speech condemning the violence on Sunday, but he’s been notably absent as it has unfolded. On Tuesday he stuck with his schedule and flew to the Gulf region.

France has presidential elections next April. Two leading contenders are Marine Le Pen of the right-wing National Rally (NR) and Jean-Luc Melenchon of the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI). Of the two, Le Pen promises to lower migration and limit welfare payments to migrants. Melenchon welcomes mass migration and opposes any reduction in benefits. Le Pen opposes illegal migration, but she hasn’t campaigned on reducing the bloated benefits bill.

>>> France’s Riots Echo 1968. But Macron Is No de Gaulle

But France’s checkbook is tapped out. It hasn’t balanced a budget in 50 years, and this year’s deficit is over 5%. Economic growth is under 1%. Diesel costs about $10 a gallon. National debt is 120% of GDP, and the bond market is getting nervous.

Like other developed countries, France’s fertility rate is below replacement, and the country has allowed in millions of immigrants from its former colonies. On balance, these new arrivals and their children have a lower employment rate than native French, but they get the same social services. Those numbers don’t work, no matter how smart the president in Paris.

Not only is France broke, but it has too few bodies to handle multiple riots at once. France’s national police handle the cities, while the gendarmes enforce the law in the countryside. Both are funded centrally by the French state. Towns have municipal police, but they aren’t equipped or trained for law enforcement, let alone riot control. France has specialized riot-control units, but only so many. The French military is probably Europe’s best, but it is not used for internal operations.

Like France, some of our major cities, New York and Seattle, are now run by avowed socialists. Arguably, administrations in Boston and Los Angeles are also closely aligned with DSA values. And more cities will be in the future.

The DSA wants open borders, nationalized health care, curtailed law enforcement, and higher taxes. If we don’t take heed, France’s present could be our future.

#7556. Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

Delaware families and policymakers are wrestling with the same issue troubling Americans nationwide: how to handle artificial intelligence.

In 2024, lawmakers in the Blue Hen State created a committee to study AI. Good thing, because parents and teachers badly need guidance on this issue.

Yet AI technology has advanced rapidly over the past two years, so the committee should prioritize drafting recommendations for K-12 schools.

To date, state officials have set only “voluntary” guardrails around AI use in elementary and secondary schools, according to the Delaware-based Caesar Rodney Institute. In May, legislators considered a proposal to create a pilot program that would allow 12 schools to use AI technology.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI

Still, the final report on the activities would not be due until 2029, and this year’s freshman class will be seniors by then. These students will be gone before lawmakers act on the report’s findings. Instead, lawmakers should focus on helping students in school today.

Besides, given the pace of change in AI technology, this proposal is too little, too late.

Fortunately, legislative models already exist that lawmakers can apply to allow the use of AI in schools, protect student data and prohibit nonacademic AI activities in classrooms.

Heritage Foundation research explains that lawmakers need not explicitly ban or allow the use of AI in schools. For school officials who allow AI in classrooms, however, educators should adopt training programs for teachers and students. These programs should help teachers and students draft prompts and questions for generative AI bots; create media using AI, such as audio, video and pictures; edit student writing; detect biases in AI results; evaluate different AI bots to decide which are the most effective; and protect student privacy.

Local school boards should adopt policies stating that students may use AI for schoolwork only when specifically allowed by teachers.

The U.S. Department of Education is urging state and local authorities to develop solutions. “Research and experience have demonstrated that technology is a valuable instructional tool when it supports strong pedagogy and effective teaching practices,” writes Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary for elementary and secondary education. “The U.S. Department of Education believes these decisions [about education technology] are best made by states and local communities.”

Policymakers should move quickly. Even if self-reported student usage numbers are slightly inflated, the share of students using AI remains remarkable.

Education officials in large school systems such as New York City and Los Angeles are attempting to prohibit the use of AI for this school year. With so many students already using bots, however, a ban on AI will be difficult to enforce.

>>> Meta Abandons Its AI-Generating Tool, but Public-Safety Guardrails Are Needed

Instead of prohibiting AI, policymakers should draw on existing research to select appropriate educational applications of the technology. For example, lawmakers should block the use of companion bots that simulate personal interactions and develop relationships with users.

Instead, educators can give students access to generative bots that use data to summarize complex information. Teachers can benefit from AI programs that help organize lesson plans. When teachers assign students to use AI, students should report how they used the technology.

Parents should have the choice to opt out of these assignments and have students complete the work using other methods.

State policymakers must focus on boosting student outcomes as technology evolves. Federal officials agree. Ms. Baesler writes: “The question should not be whether teachers and students use technology. The question should be whether the technology we ask teachers and students to use improves learning and students’ academic outcomes.”

As Delaware’s AI committee drafts recommendations, officials should focus on student success. Those on both sides of the political aisle—and on either side of AI debates—can agree on this.

Then, parents and teachers can share best practices and offer solutions to help students across all 50 states.
