#7463. ABA tracks new challenges affecting Public Service Loan Forgiveness borrowers

The ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. (Image from Shutterstock)

For lawyers and other student loan borrowers working in public service jobs, the path to having their remaining federal student loan balances discharged under Public Service Loan Forgiveness program after 120 months of qualifying payments is becoming increasingly difficult to navigate.

Under the PSLF program, created by Congress in 2007 with the support of the ABA, borrowers who have made 120 timely payments on their federal direct loans while employed full time in qualifying public service jobs are eligible to receive forgiveness of whatever portion of their loan remains after completing the payments.

But the ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. Issues include processing delays, payment record errors, growing application backlogs, and changes in Department of Education policies and procedures—some implemented with little or no public notice. Significant staffing cuts at the department, including a 40% reduction in Federal Student Aid office staff, have added to concerns about whether problems can be resolved promptly.

For reasons that are not yet clear, many borrowers have not received credit for qualifying loan repayments they’ve made since June, which means those payments cannot yet be counted toward their 120-repayment requirement. The Department of Education has not offered information or explanation on the missing information.

Separately, the Department of Education confirmed in August that it has reduced the number of some borrowers’ qualifying payments, potentially delaying when their remaining loan balances will be forgiven. After initially describing the falling payment counts as a “data issue,” the department subsequently said the changes were intentional, correcting coding errors during the Biden administration that resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers.

For example, some of the PSLF credit reversals may have been for payments made in a repayment plan that didn’t qualify for PSLF, although without an explanation from the Education Department about this process, some borrowers believe their payment counts were removed erroneously.

Without a formal announcement, the department also in July quietly eliminated the Biden-era 15-day grace period on whether PSLF-eligible payments counted as timely. As of July 1, a payment must be made “on or before the due date” to count as a qualifying payment under PSLF.

Also, a “clarification” by the department about the PSLF Buyback program is causing confusion and concern among borrowers.

The PSLF Buyback program allows public service employees to get credit toward the required 120 payments for months their loans were, e.g., in deferment or forbearance and thus not eligible for PSLF. Borrowers can apply to “buy back” those months, however, by paying what they would have paid had they been in repayment during those months.

But under updated Department of Education guidance, borrowers will not be able to buy back credit for payments made while under either of two new repayment plans—the Repayment Assistance Plan or the Tiered Standard Repayment Plan. These two new repayment plans were created in legislation signed into law by President Donald Trump in 2025.

Further causing concern is the significant application backlog for the PSLF Buyback program. As of April, the application backlog was between 70,000 to 90,000, but no new data has been released since that time. Even if the backlog has been reduced, some borrowers have waited two years or more to get credit for retroactive payments. The delay requires them to remain in their jobs and repay their loans for longer than required, thus functionally ending the buyback program.

On Oct. 21, the Department of Justice dropped its appeal of two court rulings that stayed the Department of Education’s controversial proposed rules to PSLF, which would have narrowed PSLF eligibility by excluding employees of organizations engaged in activities the department considered as having a “substantially illegal purpose.”

In August, the department had appealed the separate decisions by federal judges in Massachusetts and Washington, D.C., that had vacated the rules.

The ABA vigorously opposed the department’s proposals. In letters to Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, ABA Presidents Bill Bay and Michelle Behnke cited a lack of statutory and other legal authority. The ABA House of Delegates reinforced that opposition through adoption of Resolution 505 at its February 2026 midyear meeting, which opposes efforts to politicize this politically neutral program.

“Any perception that benefits are awarded based on political affiliation or ideology undermines the legitimacy of programs such as PSLF, discourages participation, and decreases the requisite public confidence they require to be successful,” the report accompanying the resolution states.

The ABA recognizes the crucial role PSLF plays in encouraging individuals to pursue careers that provide much-needed public services, including public defense services and civil legal aid representation to underrepresented communities such as senior citizens and veterans.

Since the program’s creation, the ABA has consistently responded to attacks and efforts to repeal or cut the program, including direct lobbying efforts through multiple Congresses and administrations; major grassroots campaigns including as a priority at past ABA Day fly-in events in Washington, D.C.; and working alongside its allies in the PSLF Coalition, a collaboration of more than 100 nonprofit and public service organizations.

In all, the ABA has adopted three policies supporting the program, including one in 2002 calling for the program’s creation. The most recent, Resolution 505, urges removal of the requirement that applicants be in qualifying employment at the time of applying for discharge of their student loans—a current program requirement that holds borrowers in limbo, unable to change jobs until the paperwork is filed. Once the required service and payment obligations are met, the resolution states, “there should be no further obligation than to apply for the benefits owed.”

As new issues with the program continue to emerge, the ABA will continue to work with allies to identify issues affecting borrowers and press for solutions. To learn more as significant developments occur, follow us at @ABAGrassroots on LinkedIn.

This report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to issues being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7461. Court finds law protecting judges, officers’ personal information unconstitutional

U.S. District Judge Esther Salas of the District of New Jersey delivers remarks at a news conference in Newark, New Jersey, on Dec. 19, 2022. (Photo By Kyle Mazza/Sipa USA/Sipa via AP Images)

A West Virginia law shielding the online publication of personal information belonging to judges and law enforcement officers was ruled unconstitutional by a federal appeals court Tuesday.

The Oct. 27 ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, is the first instance of a federal appellate court overriding a state law protecting the home addresses and unpublished phone numbers of judges and officers since states began safeguarding personal information after a gunman shot and killed 20-year-old Daniel Anderl, the son of U.S. District Judge Esther Salas of the District of New Jersey, inside their New Jersey home in 2020.

Class action lawsuits filed by Michael Jackson, a retired law enforcement officer, charged Thomson Reuters, Whitepages Inc., PeopleConnect and LexisNexis with violating the state’s Daniel’s Law through online people search services, according to coverage by Reuters.

Bursor & Fisher attorney Philip Fraietta, who represents Jackson, did not give a comment for the article.

#7457. Justice Department’s Statement on Its Investigation of Vistra’s Acquisition of Cogentrix

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. of the U.S. Department of Justice issued the following statement today in connection with the Antitrust Division’s investigation into the acquisition of Cogentrix Energy (Cogentrix) by Vistra Corp. (Vistra) (together, the “Parties”):

“Electricity customers in Maine, New Hampshire, and across New England will benefit from continued competition to generate affordable electricity. As New Englanders turn on the heat for the coming winter season, it’s critical that consumers not bear the risks of higher electricity bills. The Division anticipates that Vistra’s divestitures will save consumers throughout New England tens of millions of dollars annually in electricity bills.”

“The Division has developed sophisticated methods for reviewing electricity generation mergers; these tools benefit American consumers and businesses that depend on affordable power,” said Deputy Assistant Attorney General G. Charles Beller of the Justice Department’s Antitrust Division. “Given the importance of affordable electricity for consumers, the Division will continue to monitor electricity transactions and the electricity sector as a whole. The Division will not hesitate to take appropriate action to safeguard competition in electricity markets.”

On Jan. 5, Vistra announced an agreement to acquire Cogentrix from Quantum Capital Group. Both firms are electricity generation companies that compete in wholesale electricity and electric capacity auctions run by Regional Transmission Organizations (RTOs) or Independent System Operators (ISOs). RTOs and ISOs are nonprofit organizations responsible for managing and operating electric power grids within specific regions of the United States. These organizations also rely on internal or external market monitors, who are responsible for overseeing and evaluating the electricity market’s performance.

Vistra’s acquisition of Cogentrix combines overlapping electricity generation asset portfolios in three different RTO/ISOs: PJM Interconnection LLC (which covers portions of the Midwest and Mid-Atlantic); ISO New England Inc. (ISO-NE); and the Electric Reliability Council of Texas.

As required by federal law, Vistra and Cogentrix filed an application with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC) for approval of the transaction. During FERC’s review process, the Internal Market Monitor of ISO-NE submitted comments to FERC stating that Vistra’s acquisition of Cogentrix raised concerns about a potential reduction in competition that may enable the exercise of market power in ISO-NE. While the Parties’ FERC application was pending, Vistra unilaterally decided to sell its Casco Bay Energy facility (Casco Bay) in ISO-NE. FERC acknowledged that it “consider[ed]” Vistra’s unilateral decision and approved the transaction without conditions. Following FERC’s approval, the Division continued its investigation to assess whether Vistra would have the ability and incentive to withhold electricity from the ISO-NE market after acquiring Cogentrix, notwithstanding the Casco Bay facility divestiture.

The Division conducted a thorough investigation, reviewing thousands of documents, performing sophisticated economic modeling, and conducting extensive interviews with industry participants. After evaluating this evidence, the Division remained concerned that the portfolio of electricity generation units that would be combined in ISO-NE may result in a substantial lessening of competition, even with the sale of the Casco Bay facility. The Division’s legal and economic analysis followed the framework for evaluating electricity mergers described in the Division’s 2025 settlement complaint and competitive impact statement regarding Constellation Energy Corp.’s acquisition of Calpine Corp.

Vistra and Cogentrix then unilaterally decided to sell Cogentrix’s gas-fired combined-cycle power plant in Rumford, Maine, which would reduce the combined firm’s ability and incentive to withhold electricity and raise prices in ISO-NE. The Division will continue to monitor Vistra’s sale of the Rumford facility. In the interim period, Vistra and Cogentrix must continue to abide by all applicable FERC regulations. The Division emphasizes that the outcome of this investigation is limited to its facts.

#7454. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7453. Chemerinsky: Supreme Court once again examines conflicts over the free exercise of religion

On Tuesday, the U.S. Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in a major case about free exercise of religion, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. Over the last decade, the justices have greatly expanded First Amendment protections for religion. This case could either go much further in that direction or show a court that is willing to allow the government to stop discrimination even when it infringes on religious beliefs.

The case involves a Colorado law launched in 2023 that provides for universal preschool education. Under the program, the state will pay for preschool at any public, secular private or religious school. To receive funds, the school must agree that it will not discriminate against children based on their parents’ race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, income or lack of housing.

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, and another Catholic preschool in the Archdiocese of Denver declined to sign the agreement, saying that it conflicts with church teachings on marriage, sex and gender. Their objection is to having to agree to take children whose parents are gay, lesbian or transgender. They argue that excluding the religious schools from the universal program denies them a public benefit due to their religious beliefs.

The federal district court and the Denver-based 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected their challenge and upheld the Colorado law. Both courts relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in Employment Division v. Smith (1990), which held that the free exercise clause of the First Amendment cannot be used to require exceptions from general laws. That case involved Native Americans who sought an exemption from an Oregon law prohibiting the consumption of peyote on the grounds that its use was a part of their religious rituals. Justice Antonin Scalia wrote the opinion for the court ruling against the Native Americans. The court said that so long as the law was neutral, not motivated by a desire to infringe religion, and so long as it applied to everyone, it could not be challenged as denying free exercise of religion.

The federal district court and the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law prohibiting discrimination by preschools, concluding that it was a neutral law of general applicability. These courts also held that there was no discrimination against religious schools in their ability to receive public funds. In a series of cases—Trinity Lutheran v. Comer (2017), Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020), and Carson v. Makin (2022)—the court held that it violates free exercise of religion for the government to deny funds to religious schools that it provides to private secular schools. The Colorado law was upheld because it does not discriminate against religious schools; it provides funds to faith-based preschools on the same terms as all other preschools.

The plaintiffs sought certiorari, and the Supreme Court granted review on two questions. (1) Whether proving a lack of general applicability under Employment Division v. Smith requires showing unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct; (2) whether Carson v. Makin displaces the rule of Employment Division v. Smith only when the government explicitly excludes religious people and institutions.

The last major Supreme Court decision concerning the application of Employment Division v. Smith was Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021). The city of Philadelphia contracts with private social service agencies to help place children in foster homes. Every contract is explicit in prohibiting the agency from discriminating on the basis of race, sex, religion and sexual orientation.

Catholic Social Services long had participated in this aspect of the program but in recent years has declined to do so because of the contractual requirement that it not discriminate based on sexual orientation. CSS says that its religious beliefs prevent it from providing inspections or placing children with same sex-couples.

The agency challenged the nondiscrimination requirement as violating its First Amendment rights. The district court and the Philadelphia-based 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected these arguments. Both courts relied on Employment Division v. Smith.

The Supreme Court unanimously reversed the lower courts and ruled in favor of Catholic Social Services. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion for the court. He said that under Employment Division v. Smith a “law is not generally applicable if it ‘invite[s]’ the government to consider the particular reasons for a person’s conduct by providing a ‘mechanism for individualized exemptions.’” The Philadelphia ordinance gave city officials the authority to grant exceptions to the nondiscrimination requirement. The court said that it was irrelevant that none ever had been granted and that there was no evidence of discrimination against religious entities. The existence of discretion was enough for it to not be a neutral law of general applicability. Therefore, it had to meet strict scrutiny. The court concluded that the city failed to meet strict scrutiny and that its policy was therefore unconstitutional.

Justice Samuel Alito concurred in the judgment and was joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch. In a 77-page opinion, Justice Alito expressly called for the court to overrule Smith. Justice Alito argued at length against the Smith approach and stated: “We should reconsider Smith without further delay. The correct interpretation of the free exercise clause is a question of great importance, and Smith’s interpretation is hard to defend. It can’t be squared with the ordinary meaning of the text of the free exercise clause or with the prevalent understanding of the scope of the free-exercise right at the time of the First Amendment’s adoption.”

Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote a concurring opinion that was joined in full by Justice Brett Kavanaugh. She expressed agreement with many of the criticisms of Smith advanced by Justice Alito. But she said that there are hard questions as to what test should replace the one from Smith. She said that the court did not need to address that in this case because the city of Philadelphia policy was unconstitutional “regardless whether Smith stays or goes.”

The Supreme Court did not grant certiorari in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy on the question of whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith, but that issue very much underlies the issues before the court.

Petitioner St. Mary’s Catholic Parish clearly is urging the court to jettison Smith. The first argument in its brief is that the “court rarely applies Smith.” It says: “Out of the 18 free exercise cases this court has resolved since Smith in 1990, this court has relied on Smith only twice to rule against the religious objector,” and one of these was Smith itself.

There also is the underlying question of whether a religious belief should be a basis for an exemption from antidiscrimination laws. In Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises Inc. (1968), the court summarily rejected a claim that a person’s religious beliefs were a basis for their discriminating in violation of civil rights statutes. If the court overrules Smith, or says that strict scrutiny should be used under Smith, the question will need to be addressed: Should free exercise of religion provide a right to harm others by discriminating against them?

For decades, the Supreme Court decided cases about when government aid to religious schools violated the establishment clause of the First Amendment. But over the last decade, the court has held that the denial of funding to religious schools when it is provided to private secular schools violates the free exercise clause of the First Amendment. For example, in its most recent ruling, Carson v. Makin (2022), the court held that it violated free exercise of religion for the state to pay for secular private schools but not religious schools for children in rural areas where there are not public schools.

The district court and the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law on the ground that it provided aid to all preschools—public, secular private, and faith-based—on exactly the same terms. But St. Mary’s Catholic Parish argues that Colorado is denying it funding because of its exercising its religious beliefs and excluding children whose parents are gay, lesbian or transgender.

In the prior cases about funding, the state laws expressly excluded religious schools. The Colorado law does not do that. Is it enough for a free exercise violation that its effect is to deny funding to schools that have a religious basis for their discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity?

In recent years, the conservative majority on the Supreme Court has greatly lessened the protections of the establishment clause of the First Amendment while simultaneously significantly increasing the safeguards under the free exercise clause. It has shown support for those who want to violate anti-discrimination laws on account of their religious beliefs. St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy will be important in indicating whether the court will go even further in these directions.

Erwin Chemerinsky is dean of the University of California at Berkeley School of Law. He is an expert in constitutional law. He’s also the author of many books, including his most recent ones: Campus Speech and Academic Freedom: A Guide for Difficult Times and The Supreme Court October Term 2024: Taking Sides.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7449. Botox Fraud Doctor Sentenced to 15 Years in Prison for $45M Medicare Scheme

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

California doctor Violetta Mailyan was sentenced yesterday to 15 years in prison for using her medical practice to fraudulently bill Medicare more than $45 million for Botox injection services that were medically unnecessary and never provided.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Violetta Mailyan, 45, of Glendale, California, owned and operated Healthy Way Medical Center, a clinic that purported to provide beauty and cosmetic services.

Although Medicare reimburses medical providers for Botox injections when necessary to treat documented cases of chronic migraines, Mailyan billed and received payments for thousands of injections that were never provided, were provided only for cosmetic purposes, or were given to patients whose primary care physicians had not referred them for treatment of chronic migraines. Evidence also showed that Mailyan billed for thousands of injections, representing over $19 million, purportedly provided on days when her clinic was closed. Mailyan also billed for providing Botox injections when she was actually on vacation in Mexico, Hawaii, Las Vegas, Pennsylvania, and New York at various times throughout her fraud scheme. For example, Mailyan billed over $200,000 for purportedly providing Botox services to patients in California when she was actually relaxing on the beach in Cabo:

The evidence also showed that when Mailyan realized federal investigators were closing in, she tried to hide her tracks by falsifying medical records and forging Medicare beneficiary signatures, including for a man who was in federal prison during the time Mailyan claimed to have provided treatment. Mailyan submitted these records to federal investigators, intending to throw them off her trail and make it appear as though she had seen patients she had not actually seen.

Mailyan used the money she stole to purchase luxury goods, including a $12,000 17th century crossbow and a $3,000 painting, depicted below:

In sentencing Mailyan, the Court commented that Mailyan’s fraud “was truly breathtaking in scope and shocking in its duration,” and that her actions were “almost unbelievable in their brazenness.” In addition to the prison sentence, the Court ordered the immediate forfeiture of over $16,029,742 worth of property seized from Mailyan, including real property, personal property, securities, and bank funds, effectively returning this taxpayer money to the United States. Mailyan was also ordered to pay $32,904,049.41 in restitution to Medicare, and the United States will vigorously pursue the return of these stolen funds.

After a six-day jury trial ending in May 2026, Mailyan was convicted of nine counts of wire fraud and three counts of obstruction of a criminal investigation of a health care offense. The jury also found that Mailyan used the fraud proceeds to purchase two Tesla vehicles, including a Cybertruck, and five pieces of California real estate.

Trial Attorneys Sandor Callahan and Jeffrey A. Crapko of the Fraud Division’s Health Care Fraud Section prosecuted the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Tara Vavere for the Central District of California’s Asset Forfeiture and Recovery Section is handling asset forfeiture matters.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

The Department of Justice’s Health Care Fraud Strike Force Program, currently comprised of nine strike forces operating in federal districts across the country, has charged more than 6,200 defendants who collectively billed federal health care programs and private insurers more than $45 billion since 2007. In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. More information can be found at www.justice.gov/criminal-fraud/health-care-fraud-unit.

#7446. Racial comments to attorney sparked investigation of federal judge

U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas is accused of making racial comments to an attorney. (Photo from Facebook/Judge Ada Brown for SCOTUS)

A lawyer who filed a misconduct complaint against a federal judge in Dallas did so after a hearing during which she repeatedly directed racial insults at him, Bloomberg Law reports.

Documents show that attorney Ezra Young, who represented a Black woman professor suing over a tenure denial, filed the complaint following the April hearing in Dallas. His complaint and the response from U.S. District Judge Ada Brown of the Northern District of Texas were among the documents that Brown circulated in an Oct. 17 email to lawyers, judges and members of the media, Bloomberg Law reports.

Throughout the hearing, Brown, a Black woman with Native American ancestry, accused Young of mistreating Black attorneys, took “judicial notice” of her own background in making findings against Young, and repeatedly referred to Young, who is Latino, as being white.

“I think what’s happening here, quite candidly, is you are very intimidated for some reason, Mr. Young, with Black excellence, in light of your white mediocrity. Yeah. Right?,” Brown said, according to the transcript. “You should write that down. I mean, you—I’m—you look like a white man, right?”

“I’m not white, your honor,” Young replied, adding that he’s Latino.

Young filed the complaint, saying he thought that the judge may be suffering from a mental health condition. A judicial investigation resulted in her temporarily losing her docket earlier this month. A special judicial committee has ordered Brown to undergo a psychiatric examination as part of that investigation.

#7440. Florida Pharmacist Sentenced to Over 7 Years in Prison for Massive Illegal Oxycodone Distribution Conspiracy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

A Florida pharmacist and pharmacy owner was sentenced yesterday to 90 months in prison for her role in illegally dispensing over 300,000 oxycodone 30mg pills to pharmacy patrons who had no medical need for the drug.

According to court documents and evidence presented at trial, Olushola Yusuf, 60, of Tampa, dispensed oxycodone to nearly all of her pharmacy customers. Yusuf charged customers approximately 10 times the typical cost of the drug and required payment from them in cash. In total, Yusuf dispensed at least 335,351 pills of oxycodone 30mg during the conspiracy. Oxycodone 30mg is the maximum strength available of the drug and is both sought after and potentially dangerous due to its potency. It is typically prescribed to seriously ill patients, such as those suffering from chronic cancer pain or traumatic injuries.

Yusuf owned and operated two pharmacies, Boots LLC doing business as, Striderite (Boots) in Margate, and Chans Pharmacy Plus, Inc. (Chans) in Pembroke Pines. Yusuf distributed oxycodone 30mg pills through these pharmacies. Customers drove long distances to have Yusuf fill prescriptions that they could not get filled at any other pharmacy. Some customers paid as much as $1,300 a month in cash to Yusuf for the drugs. And some customers were drug dealers who picked up oxycodone pills purportedly on behalf of dozens of patients at a time who were not present. According to witnesses at trial, Yusuf kept the doors to her pharmacies locked during business hours, directing employees only to open the door for certain identified customers. Yusuf continued to dispense oxycodone in this way even after repeated warnings from her employees and the DEA about the dangers of her pharmacy operations.

After a two-week trial in July 2026, the jury convicted Yusuf of conspiracy to illegally distribute drugs and five counts of illegal drug distribution. Yusuf’s co-defendant, Saman Gimenez, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to illegally distribute drugs and is scheduled be sentenced later this year.

Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

In addition, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, working in conjunction with the Office of the Inspector General for the Department of Health and Human Services, are taking steps to hold providers accountable for their involvement in health care fraud schemes. #7438. Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein of New York dies at 92

In this courtroom sketch, U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York presides during a pretrial hearing in a drug trafficking case for former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, on July 22, 2026, in New York. (Photo by Jane Rosenberg via the Associated Press)

U.S. District Judge Alvin Hellerstein of the Southern District of New York died Wednesday at age 92.

Hellerstein was known for presiding over the federal narcoterrorism conspiracy case against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, according to a story from Law.com. He also oversaw more than 14,000 lawsuits that were filed by victims of the Sept. 11 terror attacks.

On a personal level, the judge is being remembered for his empathy and morality, which was informed by his Jewish faith.

“He didn’t shy away from pushing the boundaries of the law if he thought they would be unjust otherwise,” Evan Farber, a partner at Loeb & Loeb who once clerked for Hellerstein, told Law.com.

Hellerstein graduated from Columbia Law School in 1956, and he became a clerk for U.S. District Judge Edmund Palmieri of the Southern District of New York, Law.com reports. He was a military lawyer with the U.S. Army and a partner and a litigator at Stroock & Stroock & Lavan before being nominated to the federal bench by then-President Bill Clinton. He was confirmed unanimously in 1998.

He took senior status in 2011, but he never slowed down, Law.com reports.

#7437. The interim docket remains active

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The interim docket dominated court news this week. Among other developments, the court declined to allow the Trump administration to implement its new transgender inmate policy and then received a new application from the administration addressing a block on border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas. On the oral argument docket, the justices agreed to hear two significant cases – one on race and school admissions and the other on the federal ban on home distilling. They will likely be argued early next year.

Looking ahead, on Thursday, Oct. 29, at 1 p.m. EDT, Amy will join Briefly’s Adam Stofsky on LinkedIn Live to discuss what unfolded at the court this month. Register here for the event.

Three cities and a group that provides legal services to immigrants have asked the Supreme Court to pause an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice that prevents enforcement of a Biden-era rule allowing immigration judges to pause certain deportation proceedings. On Thursday, Texas and the DOJ responded to this application. For more on the filings, see the On Site section below.

Also on Thursday, the Supreme Court granted a request from election officials in New Hampshire to allow enforcement of a law that prohibits the use of student IDs for voting. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson wrote a dissenting opinion. Learn more about the dispute in the On Site section.

On Wednesday, the Supreme Court denied the Trump administration’s request for it to clear the way for the Federal Bureau of Prisons to implement its new policy on transgender inmates, which would prevent such inmates from obtaining gender-transition surgeries, hormone therapy, and “social accommodations.” Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito indicated, without explanation, that they would have granted the application.

Later on Wednesday, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. Responses to the application are due by 4 p.m. EDT on Thursday, Oct. 29.

In its Monday order list, the Supreme Court added two cases to the oral argument docket for the 2026-27 term: a challenge to the process that a Maryland county uses to determine admissions to highly selective public magnet schools and a dispute over the constitutionality of the federal ban on home distilleries. It also denied review in several high-profile cases, including on plea deals for some of the men alleged to have planned the 9/11 attacks.

The midterm elections on Nov. 3 will bring an end to “an electoral cycle shaped to an unusual degree by” Supreme Court rulings, including recent decisions on congressional redistricting and campaign finance restrictions, according to Reuters. Ilya Somin, a law professor at George Mason University, told Reuters that “Republicans seem to have gained a net benefit from” these rulings. “It remains to be seen, however, whether these legal victories will help President Donald Trump’s party in its quest to retain control of Congress.” No matter how the midterm elections turn out, additional legal battles may follow over such issues as “federal interference in the voting,” Reuters noted.

During Wednesday’s episode of “High Stakes,” a podcast featuring former presidential candidate Hillary Clinton and journalist Kara Swisher, Clinton addressed possible Supreme Court reforms, “rais[ing] some practical concerns about term limits on Supreme Court justices” but “expressing support” for adding justices, according to MS Now. “[W]e should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power,” Clinton said. “You know, it used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit. We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices. So I would be in, you know, favor of looking at that and see if we could make it work.”

Sen. Dick Durbin will retire in early January after a combined 44 years in the House and Senate. While in the Senate, he was a key figure on the Senate Judiciary Committee and took part in “confirmation hearings for eight of the nine Supreme Court justices,” according to The Washington Sun. Durbin spoke with the Sun about significant moments in his career, including when Democratic Sen. Harry Reid took “the first party-line step to break filibuster constraints” for confirming judges and Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell “blocked the 2016 nomination of Merrick Garland” to the Supreme Court. The Sun noted that Durbin is “careful not to tell his current colleagues what they should do in the future. But he’s not very supportive of trying to further blow up the institutional guardrails in order to do things now demanded by the [Democratic Party’s] most liberal faithful, such as expanding the Supreme Court.”

In his newsletter for The New York Times, Adam Liptak revisited Citizens United v. FEC, in which the Supreme Court held in 2010 “that corporations and unions have a First Amendment right to spend unlimited amounts in candidate elections.” As Liptak noted, many claim Citizens United significantly damaged American politics without fully understanding what the Supreme Court held. “[T]here are many misconceptions about Citizens United,” Liptak wrote. “A cleareyed look at the decision undermines the conventional view that it single-handedly opened the floodgates of dark money in American politics.”

In a column for Bloomberg, Noah Feldman highlighted Justice Elena Kagan’s Tuesday appearance at Catholic University’s law school in Washington, during which she criticized the conservative majority’s approach to voting rights and raised concerns that it “has kind of blinded itself to the very deleterious effects of [its] rulings on how the political system works.” Kagan, according to Feldman, “made it clear that ignoring consequences is not a mere accident but a direct result of originalism, the dominant conservative judicial philosophy.” Feldman described Kagan’s criticism as “spot on,” writing that “[w]illful blindness to real-world consequences really is at the heart of the harm the conservative majority is doing to the country.”

The Supreme Court on Thursday afternoon cleared the way for New Hampshire to bar the use of student IDs as the valid photo ID required to obtain a ballot there. In a brief, unsigned order, the justices paused a ruling by a federal judge in New Hampshire, citing the principle (often known as the Purcell principle) that “lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election.”

The Trump administration and Texas urged the Supreme Court on Thursday to leave in place their consent agreement abolishing a Biden-era regulation that had allowed immigration judges to suspend some deportation proceedings. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the justices that the request from the challengers “attempts to improperly leverage a clear-cut dispute over” the challengers’ efforts to join the case “into a far-reaching attack on the merits of” the court’s approval of the agreement. Texas argued that granting the challengers’ request “would revive a rule the district court declared unlawful, renew the fiscal and sovereign injuries Texas alleged, and unsettle a final judgment accepted by the actual parties.”

During the early months of President Donald Trump’s second term, the federal government detained and sought to deport several students and academics because of their support for Palestine. The Supreme Court could soon take up the cases of two of those detainees, Mahmoud Khalil and Badar Khan Suri, which ask whether federal trial courts have the power to consider challenges to the two men’s detentions.

In his Court Beyond Borders column, Martin Flaherty revisited the Supreme Court’s interim docket order allowing the Trump administration to deport noncitizens to countries not identified in their removal orders while a challenge to this practice continued. The decision, according to Flaherty, is representative of the court’s “increasing disregard, if not antipathy, to international human rights law.”

In his Immigration Matters column on Wednesday, César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández also explored Department of Homeland Security v. D.V.D., on “the federal government’s power to send migrants to countries where they have no ties.” He believes the court’s eventual ruling will likely focus not on the life-and-death stakes surrounding this case, but “on technical issues of judicial authority to consider the migrants’ claim[s].”

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky reflected on the Roberts court’s approach to religious freedom, highlighting recent rulings in which it “has greatly lessened the protections of the establishment clause” and “aggressively expanded the protections of the free exercise clause.” St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, which will be argued next month, “raises important questions about how far the court will go,” Chemerinsky contended.

In his Empirical SCOTUS column on Monday, Adam Feldman analyzed what could be driving President Donald Trump’s success on the emergency docket by comparing the court’s responses to applications from the past three presidential administrations (the first and second Trump administrations and the Biden administration).

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss a few orders from the Supreme Court, a CNN article on Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, and two dueling en banc decisions from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 3rd Circuit.

During a recent event in Boston, Akhil Amar engaged in a debate with retired Justice Stephen Breyer about a case Breyer sat on: the sometimes-notorious Citizens United v. FEC from 2010.

Friday’s A Closer Look is typically a judicial biography. This week we cover Justice John Catron, who served on the court from 1837 to 1865.

Justice John Catron was a man of contradictions – for example, a southern slaveholder, he also opposed the secession of Tennessee while on the court and sought to preserve the Union. At the same time, Catron remains to this day a somewhat “obscure figure,” with not one full-length biography to his name.

Catron’s birthplace and date are uncertain, with some sources putting it in Pennsylvania around 1786, and others in Virginia between 1781 and 1792. What is known is that he was born into a poor German family, had minimal schooling, married in 1807, and, by 1812, settled in Sparta, Tennessee. Not long after, Catron served as a private under then-General Andrew Jackson in the Alabama campaigns against the Creek Indians and the War of 1812, reportedly becoming so ill that he had to be brought back to Tennessee in a wagon. (Some sources say he also fought in the Battle of New Orleans.)

Catron was licensed to practice law in 1815 and then served as a prosecutor on a Tennessee “mountain circuit.” He relocated to Nashville in 1818, and soon had a thriving practice centered on land law and disputes. In 1824, the Tennessee Legislature elected Catron to the state’s Supreme Court of Errors and Appeals, then Tennessee’s highest court, where he served for seven years. His best-known ruling there was reportedly one in 1829 that disbarred a lawyer for fighting a duel in Kentucky. Catron rejected the argument that a duel amounted to an “honorable homicide” and wrote that the law treated it as “a wicked and wilful [sic] murder.” In 1831, he became the court’s first chief justice and served for three more years. As chief justice, Catron upheld the freeing of a group of enslaved people in an 1834 case, but only on the condition that they leave the United States. The next year, he upheld Tennessee’s extension of its criminal laws over Cherokee land inside the state.

Catron’s involvement in politics reportedly led to his chief justiceship ending; one scholar writes that then-presidential-candidate Hugh Lawson White’s allies forced Catron off the bench after he backed Martin Van Buren over White in the 1836 election, while another account says the legislature retaliated for his backing of Van Buren by abolishing the Court of Errors and Appeals altogether. Catron then went on to manage Van Buren’s Tennessee campaign.

Catron’s support for Van Buren and “align[ment] with Jacksonian democracy” led to Jackson nominating Catron to the Supreme Court on his last full day as president on March 3, 1837, the same day that Congress added two seats to the Supreme Court (bringing it to nine). Five days after Jackson’s nomination, with Van Buren now in the White House, the Senate confirmed Catron by a vote of 28 to 15.

Catron “never sought to take a leading part in the great public questions before the Supreme Court,” instead opting for opining on “complex technical matters” and the common law. Averaging 7.5 opinions per term (a lower rate than any Taney Court colleague except Justice James Wayne), Catron usually sided with Chief Justice Roger Taney and often took cases over Spanish land grant disputes. Catron did make clear some of his own views; in the 1853 case of Ohio Life Insurance & Trust Co. v. Debolt, he warned against the rapid growth of corporations, writing that “these numerous bodies of associated wealth” risked “stand[ing] above the state government creating them.”

Catron’s most significant moment on the court came in the 1857 case of Dred Scott v. Sandford, where he agreed in his concurrence that Congress lacked the power to prevent slavery in the western territories and that Scott remained enslaved. While the case was pending, he also wrote privately to then-president-elect James Buchanan, asking him to persuade Justice Robert Grier to join the majority (Grier ultimately did so).

Catron enslaved people throughout his life, and in 1827 he reportedly fathered a son whom he never acknowledged with Sally, an enslaved woman. However, Catron did not follow Tennessee out of the Union and in 1861 returned to Nashville to try to persuade the state’s leaders not to secede. After they declined, he left for Kentucky and his property in Tennessee was confiscated. He kept riding circuit in Kentucky and Missouri, and when the army locked up civilians who sympathized with the Confederacy, Catron turned away their requests for habeas corpus, effectively supporting the detentions. Once federal forces took control of Nashville, he went back and opened the U.S. district court there in June 1862. Catron dissented in the 1863 Prize Cases, arguing that President Abraham Lincoln could not blockade Southern ports without Congress’ approval.

Catron died in his Nashville home in May 1865, shortly after the Confederate surrender. Henry Stanbery was nominated by President Andrew Johnson to fill his seat, but the Senate did not act before Congress eliminated the seat in 1866 to keep Johnson from appointing justices.

#7436. Chief Justice John Roberts’ long game on executive power

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

One of Chief Justice John Roberts’ most enduring commitments has been to expanding presidential power. In that regard, Roberts has long opposed Congress’ limits on the president’s authority to remove the officers heading the nation’s executive agencies. Indeed, as far back as 1983, Roberts, serving in the Reagan administration, wrote a memo to the White House counsel that “the time is ripe to reconsider the constitutional anomaly of independent agencies.”

This summer, Roberts was able to turn his long-held goal into reality. Writing for the majority in Trump v. Slaughter, the court ruled that the president may unilaterally remove those officers leading nearly all of the nation’s federal independent agencies. Much has been written on this decision. But much less has been said on how Roberts carefully, and then all at once, guided the court to its decision in Slaughter. This not only provides insight into Roberts’ core conservative commitments but how he has wielded his power on a fractured court.

Central to this tale is the chipping away, and eventual reversal, of Humphrey’s Executor v. United States, a unanimous Supreme Court decision from 1935. In Humphrey’s, the court upheld congressional restrictions on President Franklin Roosevelt’s ability to remove a Federal Trade Commission commissioner, William Humphrey, who had been appointed by FDR’s predecessor, President Herbert Hoover.

Although Congress had specified that an FTC commissioner could be removed only for “inefficiency, neglect of duty, or malfeasance in office,” Roosevelt did not invoke those grounds when firing Humphrey. Instead, as the president explained to him, “I do not feel that your mind and my mind go along together on either the policies or the administering of the Federal Trade Commission.” Humphrey sued for reinstatement and ultimately prevailed before the Supreme Court, although not before passing away in 1934 (hence, Humphrey’s executor).

Throughout the 20th century, Humphrey’s sat alongside Myers v. United States, decided in 1926, in which the Supreme Court rejected the claim by a postmaster that he could not be removed from his position by the president. Myers relied on an 1867 law known as the Tenure of Office Act that required the president to obtain Senate consent before removing certain executive officers. In rejecting Myers’ claim, the court held that the postmaster was a subordinate of the president and could be removed unilaterally at will. In an opinion written by Chief Justice (and former President) William Howard Taft, the court reasoned that the president has “the exclusive power of removal” so that the president can “take care that the laws [are] faithfully executed.”

The court in Humphrey’s distinguished between “purely executive” officials (such as the postmaster in Myers) and agency officials (such as FTC commissioners) authorized by Congress to perform “quasi-judicial” and “quasi-legislative” duties. The court described this distinction as between officials assisting the president in executing the laws, on the one hand, and officials responsible for carrying “into effect legislative policies” and performing “other specified duties as a legislative or as a judicial aid.” As Professor Nathaniel Wald Donahue has explained, “Progressive Era lawyers used the categories of ‘quasi-judicial’ and ‘quasi-legislative’ to refer to administrative bodies that were understood to be executive-branch auxiliaries to the judiciary and legislature.”

In 1988, the Supreme Court applied Humphrey’s in the case of Morrison v. Olson, when it upheld the “good cause” restriction on the attorney general’s authority to remove an independent counsel appointed “to investigate and, if appropriate, prosecute certain high ranking Government officials for violations of federal criminal laws.” The court not only again credited the “distinction between ‘purely executive’ officials and officials who exercise ‘quasi-legislative’ and ‘quasi-judicial’ powers,” but rejected the argument that the removal restriction should not apply to the independent counsel engaged in the “purely executive” task of prosecution. (The lone dissenter in Morrison was Justice Antonin Scalia, who lost that battle but now has decisively won the removal power war.)

Accordingly, when Roberts became chief justice in 2005, Humphrey’s was a valid, longstanding precedent. Over the course of 16 years, through a “removal trilogy,” Roberts made sure this was no longer the case.

2010’s Free Enterprise Fund v. Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, the first case of the trilogy, involved the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, established by Congress in 2002 to regulate the accounting industry. Essentially the PCAOB was supervised by the Securities and Exchange Commission. The SEC appointed PCAOB members and could remove members, but only for “good cause shown.” By a 5-4 vote, in an opinion written by the chief justice, the court held that this dual level of protection by Congress from removal for board members violated the constitutional separation of powers.

In reaching this conclusion, Roberts employed three strategies. First, he elevated certain presidential powers over those of Congress. In particular, Roberts invoked Article II’s vesting clause, or that “the executive Power shall be vested in a President of the United States of America,” and combined this with the executive’s constitutional prerogative to “take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed.” In the chief’s words, “the President cannot ‘take Care that the Laws be faithfully executed’ if he cannot oversee the faithfulness of the officers who execute them.”

In reaching this conclusion, Roberts downplayed (1) that Congress created the PCAOB and (2) that the separation-of-powers claim at issue involved a dispute between the law Congress wrote and the president’s claimed removal authority. Roberts acknowledged that “[n]o one doubts Congress’s power to create a vast and varied federal bureaucracy.” Yet he then immediately added, “[b]ut where, in all this, is the role for oversight by an elected President?” Throughout his opinion, Roberts elevated the president’s removal authority while at the same time minimizing Congress’ legislative authority to specifically “set the terms by which” agency heads hold their positions.

The chief justice’s second strategy in Free Enterprise Fund was to apply a formalistic understanding of the separation of powers even though prior cases, including Humphrey’s Executor and Morrison, took a more functionalist approach. A formalist believes there are clear boundaries between the different branches of government and insists upon adherence to those boundaries. For Roberts, the executive branch’s responsibility to execute the laws encompasses what occurs between Congress legislating pursuant to Article I and the judiciary deciding cases under Article III – a vast province under the president’s supervision.

Formalism contrasts with functionalism, which denies the imperative of keeping the branches separate and insists upon the importance of workability in evaluating the relationship between them. In his dissent in Free Enterprise Fund, Justice Stephen Breyer, a quintessential functionalist, pressed the need for governmental flexibility to allow Congress “to respond to future ‘exigencies’” in creating agencies and designing their structure.

The third leg of Roberts’ Free Enterprise Fund opinion was his selective reading of the history of the president’s removal power. While Article II explicitly allows the president to appoint executive officers, it is silent regarding the president’s authority to remove them. Accordingly, history must be consulted. As has been canvassed extensively, the historical record is complicated. And although Breyer made this point in dissent, Roberts downplayed the debate. While the “removal of executive officers was discussed extensively” at the First Congress, Roberts breezily concluded that the “view that ‘prevailed . . .’ was that the executive power included a power to oversee executive officers through removal.”

Hence the three prongs of Roberts’ approach to attacking Humphrey’s: elevating the president’s constitutional authority to take care that the laws are executed over Congress’ authority to legislate; employing a formalistic approach to resolve the separation of powers dispute; and insisting that the historical evidence provides a conclusive answer to the question presented.

Ten years after Free Enterprise Fund, in Seila Law LLC v. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Supreme Court addressed a constitutional challenge to the structure of the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, established by Congress in response to the financial crisis in 2008. As with the PCAOB, Congress limited removal of its leadership to cause to protect the agency from the intense political pressure attendant to financial regulation. In contrast to other independent agencies led by multiple members, such as the SEC or the Federal Communications Commission, the CFPB had a single director subject to removal by the president only for “inefficiency, neglect, or malfeasance.”

The court sustained the challenge by a 5-4 vote in an opinion written by Roberts that employed essentially the same reasoning and rhetoric as in Free Enterprise Fund. Indeed, the first case cited by Roberts was Free Enterprise Fund itself, for the importance of the president’s removal authority to ensure full accountability “for discharging his own responsibilities.”

The constitutional sin of Congress’ approach in structuring the CFPB was, according to Roberts, its novelty. Leaning in even more to the formalistic, anti-innovation approach to separation of powers taken in Free Enterprise Fund, Roberts cast Myers as controlling authority and Humphrey’s as the narrow exception, stating, “[o]ur precedents have recognized only two exceptions to the President’s unrestricted removal power”: the first, Humphrey’s, involved an expert agency “led by a group of principal officers,” and the second, illustrated by Morrison, involved an inferior officer with “narrowly defined duties.” According to Roberts, Congress’ “deviat[ion]” from these precedents rendered the director’s for-cause protection from removal unconstitutional.

The Supreme Court decided Seila Law in the summer of 2020. By the time the year ended, Justice Amy Coney Barrett had succeeded Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg, giving conservatives a supermajority of six, and Joe Biden had defeated Donald Trump in the presidential election. Four years later, Trump was elected once more.

From his first day in office in 2025, Trump exercised executive power – including his removal authority – more aggressively than any of his modern predecessors. In March 2025, Trump fired the two Democratic commissioners on the Federal Trade Commission, stating “that their ‘continued service on the FTC [was] inconsistent with [his] Administration’s priorities’ and that they were removed from office ‘pursuant to [his] authority under Article II of the Constitution.’”

One of the fired commissioners, Rebecca Slaughter, filed suit. The Trump administration could not have asked for a better case to argue for overruling Humphrey’s: Slaughter had been terminated from the same agency, the FTC, that was at issue in that 1935 decision.

The issue before the court in Slaughter was broader and more consequential than the questions presented in Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law. In those earlier cases, the court evaluated the removal restrictions without addressing whether Humphrey’s should be overruled. The novelty of the agency structure designed by Congress was sufficient to strike down those restrictions. Now, if the court agreed with the administration, it would have to explain why, as a matter of stare decisis, Humphrey’s should be discarded.

With the wind of five additional votes at his back, Roberts demolished Humphrey’s. His opinion began with a historical paean to the unitary executive. The Framers vested the executive power in “a President” and insisted that there would be a single person who would sit atop the executive branch hierarchy, he wrote. Roberts acknowledged, quoting Alexander Hamilton, that the “Chief Magistrate” would have “assistants or deputies.” But to ensure accountability, those officers “must be removable by the President.”

Roberts then surveyed the governing case law – including his own. He described Myers as “scholarly” and “seminal,” rhetorically elevating this precedent. Perhaps most importantly, Roberts applied his broad understanding of executive power to repudiate Humphrey’s. He explained that the current FTC on which Slaughter served is different from the agency described by the court in 1935. According to Roberts, since “its creation in 1914, the FTC has accumulated vast rulemaking, enforcement, and adjudicatory powers” that involve it in the execution of the law. Because the FTC is now engaged in the “President’s constitutional role,” the agency must be “controlled by the Chief Executive” and commissioners must be removable at will. “If anything more is left of Humphrey’s,” Roberts wrote, “we overrule it.”

In doing so, Roberts finally subordinated the vast majority of executive agencies to the president’s will.

So, what exactly, does this tell us about the chief justice?

First, Roberts knows how to play the long game, having done so for years on the court and more than four decades as a lawyer. To be sure, Roberts had help along the way. Justice Brett Kavanaugh, who worked in the White House when George W. Bush was president, played a role in developing the court’s jurisprudence in this area. As a judge on the U.S. Courts of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, Kavanaugh wrote dissenting opinions that ultimately were upheld in Free Enterprise Fund and Seila Law. (As a justice, Kavanaugh voted with the majority in both Seila Law and Slaughter.) Trump is, of course, a critical figure in this story as well – most notably through his executive actions and his appointment of three justices (Justice Neil Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Justice Amy Coney Barrett) sympathetic to Roberts’ position on presidential power.

Second, there are limits to even Roberts’ commitment to executive authority over the independent agencies. He also wrote the court’s opinion in Trump v. Cook, decided the same day as Slaughter, in which the court made it clear that the statutory restriction on removing a Federal Reserve governor remained valid. Roberts justified this exception for the Federal Reserve on the basis of “history and tradition.” As Roberts wrote in Cook, “the Government concedes, Congress limited the President’s power to remove Governors for good reason – ‘[t]o preserve the independence of the Federal Reserve’ and to continue the ‘long tradition’ of ‘monetary policy . . . exercised independent of . . . executive influence.’” Accordingly, Roberts elaborated, any “change in that scheme must come from Congress, not the courts.” (Justice Clarence Thomas vigorously challenged Roberts’ historical account and reasoning.)

Finally, and relatedly, the removal trilogy illuminates the chief justice’s careful dance between his professed institutionalism and his core conservative commitments. In the first part of the trilogy, Roberts confined Humphrey’s but did not squarely question its validity. Subsequently, with the benefit of his own precedent and a supermajority, Roberts did not need to check his fidelity to the president’s unfettered removal authority. Indeed, Roberts may have figured out how to square this circle, taking an institutionalist approach to lead the court in its adoption of fundamental conservative principles. As the justices consider cases this term involving climate change, assault weapons, and religious freedom, we will see how fully – and at what pace – Roberts continues to embrace this strategy in his leadership of the court.

Rodger D. Citron is the Associate Dean for Research and Scholarship and Professor of Law at Touro University, Jacob D. Fuchsberg Law Center.

Recommended Citation: Rodger Citron, Chief Justice John Roberts’ long game on executive power, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 23, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/chief-justice-john-roberts-long-game-on-executive-power/
