#7435. The Ten Commandments, classroom walls, and the establishment clause

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

The Supreme Court will soon consider whether to review the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit’s full panel decision upholding a Texas law requiring a poster of the Ten Commandments to hang in public school classrooms (as well as a somewhat similar case in Louisiana). The Supreme Court need not take this case, but it was rightly decided. The 5th Circuit used the correct “historical practices and understandings” test to analyze this establishment clause challenge and reached the right result that the Texas law is constitutional. I want to focus on one part of its ruling in particular: That a text with religious origins can over time develop an additional nonreligious message which public schools can acknowledge with passive displays in classrooms. Here, Texas’ decision to hang the Ten Commandments in its classrooms does not promote religion but acknowledges its foundational role in American law.

In its 2022 decision of Kennedy v. Bremerton School District, the Supreme Court announced a new test for the establishment clause. There, the majority discarded what is known as the “Lemon Test” (named for the 1971 decision of Lemon v. Kurtzman) to determine whether state action violates the establishment clause, which had asked courts to consider whether such action had a “secular purpose”; whether it had the “principal or primary effect” of “advanc[ing]” religion; and whether the action contributed to “excessive government entanglement” with religion. In Kennedy, the court replaced this convoluted test with a more originalist one that looked at “the historical practices and understandings” of what established churches actually did under law as governmental entities.

The 5th Circuit applied that new test in the challenge to S.B. 10, the Texas law enacted in June 2025, requiring public elementary and secondary schools to display in each classroom a “durable poster or framed copy of the Ten Commandments.” The display must be at least 16x20 inches, easily readable, displayed in a conspicuous place, and must only include the text of the Ten Commandments and nothing else. The schools can acquire these displays either by accepting compliant, privately donated displays, or purchasing compliant displays using district funds.

Shortly after its passage, numerous parents of varying religious backgrounds sued several Texas school districts claiming S.B. 10 violated the establishment clause and the free exercise clause of the First Amendment. In Nathan v. Alamo Heights Independent School District, the 5th Circuit, sitting en banc, upheld Texas’ law. Specifically, the 5th Circuit found that S.B. 10 did not violate the establishment clause because it punishes no one who rejects the Ten Commandments, requires no religious exercise or observance, and neither catechizes students on the Ten Commandments nor encourages them to adopt them. The 5th Circuit reasoned that, while “[p]laintiffs have sincere religious disagreement with its content . . . that does not transform the poster into a summons to prayer.”

In upholding the Texas law, the 5th Circuit considered the Supreme Court’s 1980 decision in Stone v. Graham, where the high court ruled unconstitutional a Kentucky law that required posting of the Ten Commandments in public schools. Because Stone relied on the Lemon test to rule against the Ten Commandments in the Kentucky classrooms, the 5th Circuit followed the Supreme Court's later directive in Kennedy that it was abandoning the Lemon test and its progeny. “With Lemon extracted, there is nothing left of Stone,” the 5th Circuit concluded.

The Nathan court’s opinion demonstrates how to adhere to the Supreme Court’s ruling in Kennedy, which asks courts to “reference … historical practices and understandings” in order to interpret the establishment clause so as to “faithfully reflect[] the understanding of the Founding Fathers.” As the 5th Circuit recognized, this requires asking “a question rooted in the past: does the law at issue resemble a founding-era religious establishment?”

When Congress and the state legislatures enacted the First Amendment’s establishment clause in 1791, people generally understood what an established church did given their presence in many of the states and European countries. At its core, the establishment clause forbade Congress (and later the states, with the passage of the 14th Amendment in 1868) from enacting laws that formally coerced people to participate in the activities of a particular church.

Those challenging the Texas law argue that the religious origins of the Ten Commandments mean it is unconstitutional to place them in a public school that impressionable youth are required by state law to attend, and doing so thus at least implicitly “coerces” these students into religious participation.

This argument has several flaws (as pointed out by the 5th Circuit), but I believe its most fundamental error is to assume that the Ten Commandments can only have one meaning and that meaning is always religious. Indeed, this flies in the face of the Supreme Court’s own statement that a religious symbol like the Ten Commandments can acquire over time an additional nonreligious meaning.

In the 2019 case of American Legion v. American Atheist Association (which was brought by the First Liberty Institute), the court considered whether Maryland violated the establishment clause by maintaining a memorial to deceased World War I veterans that was in the shape of a cross. Obviously, a cross signifies the crucifixion of Jesus Christ. Nevertheless, the court, in an opinion by Justice Samuel Alito, decided that the memorial could stand, as over time the cross had gained additional nonreligious meanings of marking where someone had died in battle so as to honor their ultimate sacrifice in war. The mothers who erected the cross did not do so to promote Christianity, but to honor those from Prince George’s County, Maryland, who died while serving in World War I.

To bolster its ruling, the Supreme Court pointed to the Ten Commandments as another example of a religious symbol that has acquired an additional nonreligious meaning over time:

As the court recognized, its very courtroom has a huge carved figure of Moses holding the Ten Commandments, with brass latticed screens on both sides of the courtroom filled with small imprints of the Ten Commandments. This is not because the Supreme Court desires to promote (or coerce others into adopting) the religious message of the Ten Commandments; rather, this is to acknowledge that the Ten Commandments serve as a foundation for the Anglo-American legal system.

Others have long echoed Alito’s words that the Ten Commandments “have historical significance as one of the foundations of our legal system.” John Quincy Adams wrote to his son that “[t]he law given from Sinai was a civil and municipal as well as a moral and religious code; it contained many statutes adapted to that time only, … but many others were of universal application—laws essential to the existence of men in society, and most of which have been enacted by every nation which ever professed any code of laws.” William Blackstone wrote in his Commentaries on the Laws of England that “all human laws” depend on “natural law and divine law.” Blackstone defined divine law to be precepts “found only in the holy scriptures.” He then gave as an example “the case of murder” which he said “is expressly forbidden by the divine.”

In 1997, the Senate and the House of Representatives passed concurrent resolutions that stated in part that “the Ten Commandments have had a significant impact on the development of the fundamental legal principles of Western Civilization.” And during oral argument in the American Legion case, even Monica Miller, the attorney for the American Humanist Association challenging the World War I memorial, conceded that “the Ten Commandments … [is] basically shorthand for law itself,” because of its “dual secular meaning.”

Those challenging the Ten Commandments posters in the classrooms assume that the religious content of the Ten Commandments renders them constitutionally toxic, while refusing to recognize their additional nonreligious message.

Nor is such a dual message uncommon in public schools. Think of a public school teaching a unit on the Civil War. A teacher hangs on the wall Abraham Lincoln’s famous words, “a house divided against itself cannot stand.” But wait! Lincoln was quoting the words of Jesus from Mark 3:25. Also during that Civil War unit, say the teacher hangs the lyrics of the Battle Hymn of the Republic, adopted by Union supporters and opponents of slavery as their rallying song. It started as a Christian hymn: “Mine eyes have seen the glory of the coming of the Lord.” It would be constitutional overkill for a court to order a public school studying the Civil War to remove from the walls Lincoln’s quote and the Battle Hymn of the Republic just because they have religious origins.

Of course, that is not all. If religious materials in public schools inherently violate the establishment clause because it is irrelevant that they have an additional meaning, how could teachers ever have students study the anti-slavery speeches of Frederick Douglass, or Martin Luther King Jr.’s Letter from the Birmingham Jail, or view Renaissance art, or sing African-American spirituals or Handel’s Messiah? It would also be questionable for the school to hang posters on the classroom walls telling students to love their enemies, or to go the extra mile to help someone, or to do unto others as you would have them do unto you, all words expressed by Jesus in the Bible.

In the cross case, the Supreme Court gave another example of words that began with religious meaning and over time added a nonreligious meaning: the names of U.S. cities, like Bethlehem, Pennsylvania; Las Cruces, New Mexico; Providence, Rhode Island; Corpus Christi, Texas, etc. As the Supreme Court made clear, those city names do not violate the establishment clause – and it would be absurd to think otherwise. But under the establishment clause theory of those challenging the Ten Commandments law, it is hard to see how one could draw a line here and hang the name of their school district in classrooms without violating the First Amendment. Either words can have two meanings, or else the St. Paul (Minnesota) Public Schools better start sandblasting its name from the schoolhouse walls.

One common reaction might be that the Ten Commandments not only address universal moral principles but also certain tenets more specific to Judaism and Christianity, such as having no other gods before the one God or a prohibition of graven images of Him. But those commandments do not cancel out the fact that the Ten Commandments collectively have served as a foundation for the Western legal tradition. Texas also designed its law so that public schools cannot use the posters to proselytize or coerce students to believe them, or to punish those who do not. A Hindu student, for example, could read the Ten Commandments and conclude that her family lives in a nation where most people believe in monotheism, not the polytheism of her family, and also realize that the Founding Fathers’ religious beliefs helped form a Constitution that protects all Americans, including her. That Constitution forbids any religious tests for people seeking public office, prohibits a state church that compels belief or punishes dissent, and protects everyone’s right to freedom of speech, belief, and conscience.

All of this is to say, passive displays with religious origins have not historically been viewed as establishment clause violations, especially when the display has a second, nonreligious meaning. The same can be said about S.B. 10.

Jordan Lorence is Senior Counsel for First Liberty Institute in Washington, D.C. He has worked on many Supreme Court First Amendment cases.

Recommended Citation: Jordan Lorence, The Ten Commandments, classroom walls, and the establishment clause, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 23, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/the-ten-commandments-classroom-walls-and-the-establishment-clause/

#7432. Ohio Supreme Court suspends law license of attorney convicted of voting multiple times

The Ohio Supreme Court on Monday suspended the law license of a man convicted of illegally voting in Ohio and Florida in 2020 and 2022. (Image from Shutterstock)

The Ohio Supreme Court on Monday suspended the law license of a man convicted of illegally voting in both Ohio and Florida in 2020 and 2022.

James Saunders, a former attorney for the IRS, was convicted of two felony counts of illegal voting after casting ballots in both Cuyahoga County, Ohio, and Broward County, Florida, during the 2020 and 2022 general elections. His last known business address is in Washington, D.C., according to the state supreme court in its Oct. 26 order.

The state supreme court imposed the suspension after Saunders failed to answer a disciplinary complaint filed by the Cleveland Metropolitan Bar Association, according to a story by Cleveland.com.

Saunders had previously been disbarred in Florida. His suspension in Ohio is indefinite, the Ohio Supreme Court said, and he “will not be reinstated to the practice of law in Ohio until such time as respondent is reinstated to the practice of law in the state of Florida.”

#7429. When the Supreme Court blessed zoning

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

James Metzenbaum was stuck on a train from Washington – slowed by a snowstorm – convincing himself that his opponent had successfully persuaded the Supreme Court against his position within the last few minutes of oral argument. He had just argued in Village of Euclid v. Ambler Realty in defense of the city’s zoning plan. The poor weather meant he might not get back to his office in time to send a telegram asking Chief Justice William Howard Taft for more briefing before the weekend. So he improvised – opening the train car door, making eye contact with a man shoveling snow near the tracks, and tossing him a telegram wrapped in cash. The shoveler seems to have understood what was intended. He sent off the telegram, and a few days later the court granted Metzenbaum permission to file another brief.

Not long after that, the court granted a full rehearing, which was followed by a dramatic reversal in several justices’ positions. In a 6-3 decision, the court sided with Metzenbaum and in favor of Euclid’s power to pass comprehensive zoning, and against a local developer who had argued the town’s plan exceeded the city’s police power and destroyed the property’s value. Three justices dissented, though they never said why.

It was an odd start to the birth of modern zoning, and it happened almost exactly 100 years ago.

Many people think the term “Euclidean zoning” takes its name from the Greek “father of geometry.” Instead, it takes its name from Village of Euclid, which upheld the power of cities to zone.

But the city at the center of that lawsuit was, in fact, named after the ancient mathematician. In 1796, six surveyors working in the Western Reserve in Ohio demanded better terms for their punishing work. Together they secured an agreement to jointly own a township in return for settling a few dozen families there. They named it for the man regarded as their profession’s patron saint. And while they eventually abandoned the town’s frigid winters, the name endured.

By the early 20th century, nearby Cleveland had become an industrial metropolis and Euclid was positioned to develop alongside it. Ambler Realty owned 68 acres between Euclid Avenue, a major road for storefronts, and the Nickel Plate railroad, a hub of industrial freight – meaning the property had enormous industrial potential. But in 1922, Euclid adopted an ordinance dividing the village by use, height, and area. Near the avenue, Ambler’s land could accommodate single- and two-family dwellings, but not apartments, shops, or factories, which were relegated farther back toward the tracks. The company alleged that land worth $10,000 an acre for industry would fetch no more than $2,500 for residential use.

Ambler challenged the ordinance under the Ohio Constitution and the 14th Amendment’s due process and equal protection clauses. Government could protect health and safety, Ambler said, but it could not confiscate an owner’s freedom to use its property when the property itself posed no danger to the public.

Comprehensive zoning was still a relatively new experiment. New York City’s influential 1916 resolution, which (among other things) sought to regulate the size and height of the city’s buildings, was only a decade old when Euclid reached the Supreme Court. To supporters, zoning promised to bring scientific order to urban growth. To opponents, it entrusted the future of a city to officials who could mistake their preferences for the public welfare or succumb to lobbying.

Ambler retained Newton D. Baker, a former Cleveland mayor and Woodrow Wilson’s secretary of war during World War I. In overlapping litigation, he represented a Jewish orphanage seeking to build in University Heights, Ohio, where land-use restrictions became a tool of ethnic exclusion. Baker was thus acutely aware that a debate about the “residential character” of the city might actually be a debate about the people who wanted to reside there. Euclid’s attorney, meanwhile, was James Metzenbaum, who had helped draft the ordinance he was defending and lived on Euclid Avenue himself.

The first round went to Baker. Federal District Judge David Westenhaver, Baker’s former law partner, struck down the ordinance in 1924. According to Westenhaver, the ultimate effect of Euclid’s plan was “to classify the population and segregate them according to their income or situation in life.” But in defending the rights of both the poor and property owners, Westenhaver revealed his own prejudices: He argued that Euclid’s plan could not possibly be constitutional given that the Supreme Court had just struck down exclusionary racial zoning, which he believed was even more beneficial.

The village took advantage of a rule allowing it to appeal directly to the Supreme Court, which heard argument on Jan. 27, 1926, in the old Senate chamber (the court would move to its current location in 1935). Only eight justices were present, since George Sutherland was resting in Charleston, South Carolina, with high blood pressure.

Neither party requested a transcript, so no one knows exactly what was said at argument. But Metzenbaum later recalled a lighter moment. After Chief Justice William Howard Taft asked why Metzenbaum alternated between the term “realtors” and “real estate men,” Justice Oliver Wendell Holmes interjected that, judging from a case heard the previous week, one received more money than the other. Metzenbaum responded, “I presumed the distinction was about the same as that which exists between a statesman and a politician.” In Metzenbaum’s recollection, Taft shook with laughter, repeating the comparison.

By the time Baker finished his turn arguing, however, Metzenbaum’s good humor had evaporated. His anxiety followed him onto the train home, and, believing that Baker had misrepresented certain facts, he composed the telegram which would reach Taft by way of the snow shoveler. His worries were evidently justified. Justice Harlan Stone’s records show a 5–3 conference vote against the ordinance. But the court later agreed to hear the case again, perhaps so that Sutherland could sit for argument. The case was reargued on Oct. 12, almost exactly a century ago.

Additional argument admitted additional briefing. Cincinnati lawyer and planning advocate Alfred Bettman had missed the original amicus deadline. He sought permission to file late from Taft, whom he knew personally, and the court granted it, allowing his brief to be considered before the next argument date.

Bettman’s theory differed from Metzenbaum’s in important ways. The village’s lawyer argued for an expanding understanding of the state’s police power that would allow the government not just to regulate for public health and safety, but to promote the general welfare. Bettman, by contrast, argued that zoning was just like other nuisance laws, except it allowed localities to prevent nuisances from occurring in advance. Bettman’s theory threatened to say the quiet part out loud: certain defenders of zoning considered some people, rather than their property, a nuisance.

On Nov. 22, 1926, Sutherland announced the decision upholding Euclid’s ordinance. Taft joined him, along with Justices Holmes, Louis Brandeis, Edward Sanford, and Stone. Justices Willis Van Devanter, James McReynolds, and Pierce Butler dissented, but left no written opinion explaining why.

Sutherland’s most memorable illustration came from nuisance law: “A nuisance may be merely a right thing in the wrong place—like a pig in the parlor instead of the barnyard.” It was not exactly a flattering analogy for those who wanted to live in the type of higher-density housing banned by Euclid’s zoning ordinance. Later, Sutherland described an apartment “very often” as “a mere parasite,” benefiting from the surroundings its presence would undermine. Apartments could obstruct air and sunlight, generate traffic and noise, diminish the attractiveness of neighboring homes, and reduce the area’s residential character, he said. Though the plan would burden some businesses and owners who were not nuisances themselves, such overbreadth didn’t render the law unconstitutional on its face. (Interestingly, Sutherland mentioned how suppressing density was a means of suppressing fires, a rationale that San Francisco had used to systematically exclude primarily Chinese-owned laundries from the area and that was rejected by the Supreme Court.)

While Ambler had argued the plan was diverting industrial development away from Euclid, Sutherland concluded it had merely confined that development to certain areas. And while Euclid was engaging in a relatively new and more intrusive form of regulating property, Sutherland (quoting another opinion) responded that, “[w]ith the growth and development of the State, the police power necessarily develops … to meet the changing conditions.”

At the same time, the majority left room for future challenges. Sustaining the ordinance’s general framework did not validate every zoning plan or every application. Two years later, Sutherland himself wrote for a unanimous court in Nectow v. City of Cambridge, invalidating a residential restriction where the factual findings showed no substantial relationship to public health, safety, convenience, or welfare.

But since then, courts have overwhelmingly approved zoning and afforded localities considerable deference in crafting it.

Baker died on Christmas Day in 1937. The law firm that he helped found and that bears his name, Baker Hostetler, is one of the largest firms in the country, and buildings ranging from a public high school to a college dorm to a veteran’s hospital are named in his honor.

Metzenbaum turned his victory into a lasting professional identity, publishing “The Law of Zoning” in 1930. His wife, Bessie, had died in 1920, and he reportedly died on New Year’s Eve in 1960 trying to free his car from a snowbank while visiting her mausoleum.

Despite Euclid’s best laid plans, Ambler’s property eventually went to industrial use after all. During World War II, the federal government acquired the site to put up an aircraft engine and landing gear factory. The industrial complex now known as Nickel Plate Station sold for $18.5 million in June 2026. Apparently zoning could not predict what the community would need in the future.

A century after Euclid, the battle over zoning rages on. Proponents of zoning, as in Euclid, see it as a critical means of promoting public welfare and the surrounding environment. Opponents point to ample evidence that zoning has been used to exclude “undesirable” populations from certain parts of town, all while suppressing dynamism and inflating the cost of housing.

We have seen several Supreme Court cases establishing limits around zoning. In cases like Nollan v. California Coastal Commission and Dolan v. City of Tigard, the court limited the types of demands the government can make of property owners who apply for a development permit. And in Moore v. Cleveland, the court invalidated a zoning restriction that prevented a grandmother from living with her grandchildren. While the majority relied on the sanctity of the family, Justice John Paul Stevens wrote separately to emphasize that Euclid had “vastly diminished the rights of individual property owners,” but had not “totally extinguish[ed] them,” and thus zoning restrictions must have a meaningful relationship to the public welfare. But Euclid itself remains on firm ground, its holding having produced no written dissents but perhaps a century of consequences worth dissenting from.

Anastasia Boden is a Senior Attorney at the Pacific Legal Foundation, where she brings civil rights lawsuits that advance the Constitution’s promises of equality and economic opportunity.

Recommended Citation: Anastasia Boden, When the Supreme Court blessed zoning, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 26, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/when-the-supreme-court-blessed-zoning/

#7428. The Supreme Court as agent of the people

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In my first two entries for this column, I focused on the president’s removal power and Congress’ power to make law. This third entry focuses on our third branch of government and explains why the Supreme and inferior federal courts are properly conceptualized as faithful agents of We the People – not faithful agents of Congress. Recognizing the distinction helps explain why the Supreme Court can, and should, exercise the power of judicial review – something which, while an acknowledged part of the Supreme Court’s power for well over two centuries, has recently come under question.

Although many schools of interpretation can embrace the idea that federal courts are faithful agents of We the People, that conception of the judicial role has become a prominent feature of modern textualism. In 2017, then-Judge Amy Coney Barrett explained that “[t]he textualist commitment” to interpreting laws according to the perspective of an ordinary reader “might be explained by a … conception of faithful agency … that understands courts to be the faithful agents of the people rather than of Congress.” For support, she noted that Justice Antonin Scalia “did not think that a commitment to legislative supremacy casts courts in the role of Congress’s agents,” as he “characterized courts as agents of the people rather than agents of Congress.”

More recently, in an opinion joined by Justice Samuel Alito, Justice Neil Gorsuch defended the major questions doctrine – a canon of interpretation that requires administrative agencies to identify extra clear statutory authority before regulating in economically or politically “major” ways – by quoting then-Professor Barrett for the proposition that “clear-statement rules help courts ‘act as faithful agents of the Constitution.’”

As an initial terminological matter, there is not currently a meaningful difference between conceptualizing courts as faithful agents of the People and conceptualizing courts as faithful agents of the People’s Constitution. The Constitution’s Preamble describes the Constitution as being enacted on behalf of We the People. So under our present constitutional order, acting as a faithful agent of the People’s Constitution is a means of acting as a faithful agent of the People.

Although that conception of the judicial role has been widely held, it is nonetheless mistaken for at least three reasons.

First, the three federal branches are coequal; none is a principal or agent of the others. Second, and as I recently explained in this column, the Constitution does not empower Congress to ordinarily make law alone. Instead, Congress makes law through a multi-branch lawmaking process that includes the president. A federal jurist who claims to be a faithful agent of Congress therefore approaches statutory interpretation from a starting posture that mistakenly favors one of the two political branches that the People’s Constitution tasks with collectively making law.

The third reason why it is mistaken to conceptualize courts as faithful agents of Congress is that Congress can sometimes work with the president to make unconstitutional statutes. In those situations, federal judges who conceptualize themselves as faithful agents of Congress would seem to be required to dutifully give legal effect to Congress’ unconstitutional statutes. But that is not what courts should do if they wish to respect the Constitution’s limits. Instead, when courts are faced with constitutionally defective statutes, courts should exercise judicial review and demonstrate that the courts are themselves constitutionally prohibited from treating unconstitutional statutes as valid law. By doing so, courts demonstrate that they are faithful agents to the People’s Constitution, not Congress.

Federal courts’ power of judicial review is no doubt familiar to most lawyers, given Chief Justice Marshall’s 1803 decision in Marbury v. Madison. Less than 15 years after the ratification of the Constitution that vested “judicial Power” in the Supreme and inferior federal courts, Marshall explained that “[i]t is emphatically the province and duty of the Judicial Department to say what the law is,” and that if “the Constitution is superior to any ordinary act of the Legislature, the Constitution, and not such ordinary act, must govern the case to which they both apply.”

The familiar form of judicial review reflected in Marbury is consistent with the idea that federal courts are faithful agents of the People. Nevertheless, in an important new book, titled “Supremacy: How Rule by the Court Replaced Government by the People,” law professors Nikolas Bowie and Daphna Renan challenge the Supreme Court’s ability to review the constitutionality of federal legislation. The book offers an important argument against judicial review of federal statutes. And that argument would no doubt be of interest to constitutional framers working on a clean slate. But when it comes to working within the constitutional system already established on behalf of We the People, the book’s argument against judicial review is problematic.

The core of the problem with Bowie’s and Renan’s argument against judicial review of federal statutes is their suggestion that Congress has seemingly unlimited discretion to define its own constitutional limits. Bowie and Renan highlight, for example, the claim that “the only power the Constitution gives judges is ‘the judicial Power,’ which is a term that historically referred to British judges’ power to enforce, not second-guess, laws passed by Parliament,” and they contend that “[t]he most straightforward method of overcoming judicial supremacy would be for Congress to enact a statute that prohibits courts from enjoining or declining to enforce a federal law on constitutional grounds.” But as I have noted in earlier scholarship, such arguments risk conflating the “distinction between a supreme English Parliament and a legally constrained, coequal Congress.”

As the English constitutional theorist A.V. Dicey explained, “[t]he principle of Parliamentary sovereignty means” that “no person or body is recognised by the law of England as having a right to override or set aside the legislation of Parliament.” To recognize in Congress a power to statutorily prohibit the courts from declining to enforce a federal law on constitutional grounds would be to recognize in Congress a power that is not meaningfully distinguishable from the aspect of sovereignty that Dicey ascribes to Parliament. But as Justice Clarence Thomas has explained, “one of the fundamental differences between our Government and the British Government” is that although “Parliament was supreme[,] Congress is not.”

To be clear, conceptualizing federal courts as faithful agents of the People would not require accepting a form of judicial supremacy – or the idea that, even outside of the bounds of federal courts’ jurisdiction, every judicial opinion is binding law on the other two branches. To the contrary, the Constitution’s supremacy clause encodes a form of legislative supremacy into our constitutional order; so long as federal statutes are “made in Pursuance” of the Constitution, those statutes qualify as the “supreme Law of the Land” and thus can legitimately constrain executive and judicial decisionmaking.

But to conclude the Constitution establishes a form of legislative supremacy is distinct from concluding that the Constitution establishes a form of congressional supremacy. Unlike the sovereign Parliament, which Dicey described as having the “right to make or unmake any law whatever,” the non-sovereign Congress cannot enact whatever legislation it wants. Rather, Congress is constrained by the People’s Constitution. The supremacy clause illustrates this by, as mentioned, only treating some statutes – namely, those “made in Pursuance” to the Constitution – as the “supreme Law of the Land.” Courts thus act as proper agents of the People when they distinguish between statutes made in pursuance to the Constitution, which courts must treat as supreme law, and statutes that violate the Constitution, which the courts should set aside for purposes of resolving the case at hand.

One might nonetheless contend that judicial review of federal legislation is somehow inappropriate on democratic grounds. One version of that objection might contend that courts should act as agents of the democratically elected Congress – meaning that courts should enforce whatever statutes survive the democratic lawmaking process, even if a court concludes that the statutes violate the Constitution. Bowie and Renan, for example, argue for “democratic constitutionalism,” which they say means “a Constitution whose questions are decided not by the Court but by the people’s elected representatives through federal statutes.”

That type of argument has at least two key weaknesses.

First, federal judges are themselves selected and supervised through democratic means. To wit, federal judges are selected by a politically accountable president and confirmed by a politically accountable Senate. Federal judges may be impeached through the political impeachment process. Federal judges’ statutory rulings can largely be overruled through the democratic process with new legislation. And federal judges’ constitutional rulings can be overruled through the constitutional amendment process.

Second, and more fundamentally, the fact that federal judges do not stand for election is a constitutional feature, not a bug. In establishing the federal government, We the People tasked three coequal branches to act as the People’s agents; two branches (i.e., Congress and the president) stand for regular elections, while the third (i.e., the judiciary) does not. The fact that federal judges do not stand for election does not mean those judges are somehow not agents of the People. To the contrary, it simply means that the courts make up a different class of agents. And political minorities no doubt recognize the wisdom in empowering at least one class of agents to operate outside the daily whims of majoritarian politics.

Finally, it is of course the case that federal judges can get the law wrong – and as human beings, judges (like other humans) have the capacity to act immorally. (Bowie and Renan demonstrate as much by highlighting grave errors made by the Supreme Court throughout its history.) But Congress and the president can make legal and moral errors as well. So imposing a form of congressional supremacy would not fix the underlying problem that humans (even those that serve in Congress) are not angels. Part of the wisdom behind our Constitution’s structure is that it addressed human nature by limiting the consequences attributable to any one branch’s errors. And the courts play an important role within that constitutional design by exercising judicial review.

In sum, it is mistaken to conclude that accepting the validity of judicial review requires accepting rule by the courts rather than rule by the People. The courts, like Congress and the president, are agents of the People. And the courts rightfully act as agents of the People when they decline to give legal effect to statutes that violate the People’s Constitution.

Chad Squitieri is an Associate Professor of Law at The Catholic University of America, where he researches and teaches about federal administrative law and the Constitution's separation of powers.

#7425. Another Trump term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

President Donald Trump and his policies were a consistent and high-profile theme during the Supreme Court’s last term. The justices weighed in on several of Trump’s signature initiatives, from sweeping global tariffs and his efforts to limit the availability of birthright citizenship to his attempts to fire members of the Federal Trade Commission and Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors – as well as various important immigration cases. And that’s all before you get to the court’s interim docket, where Trump chalked up a number of significant victories.

As it currently stands, the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor, featuring two challenges to Trump’s immigration policies and a dispute over access to information about Trump’s U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE. But that could change soon: between Nov. 6 and mid-January, the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review filed by the Trump administration or Trump himself. Given the Office of the Solicitor General, which represents the federal government before the Supreme Court, has a high success rate – usually somewhere around 60% – for petitions that it files with the justices, Trump could once again end up dominating the term.

Immigration is already a hot topic on the court’s docket, but two immigration disputes could raise the prominence of the issue even more. When the justices meet for their Nov. 6 conference, one of the cases that they will consider is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, a challenge to a Trump administration policy of quickly removing immigrants who cross the border illegally without giving them the chance to seek asylum.

Two federal courts in Washington, D.C., agreed with the challengers – a group of immigrants and three immigrants’ rights groups – that the policy violates federal immigration law. That prompted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer to come to the Supreme Court in August, where he argued that the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit “threatens to dismantle” what Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin “describes as an ‘indispensable’ tool for controlling the border.”

Last month, the Trump administration asked the justices to weigh in on another dispute arising from its immigration agenda – this time involving the government’s efforts to detain and deport several students and academics because of their support for Palestine. The government’s petition came in the case of one of those detainees, Badar Khan Suri, an Indian national who came to the United States for a postdoctoral fellowship at Georgetown University. The Trump administration has told the justices that they should also consider granting the petition for review filed recently by Mahmoud Khalil, an Algerian national who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria and became a lawful permanent resident of the United States in 2024. The government contended that both men should be deported based on determinations by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that their conduct – alleged support for the Islamic militant group Hamas, in Suri’s case, and participation in “antisemitic protests and disruptive activities” for Khalil – compromised U.S. foreign policy.

Attorneys for Suri and Khalil went to federal court in New Jersey and Virginia, asking judges there to review the legality of their detentions on the ground that (among other things) they had been detained in retaliation for their speech. As their cases come to the court, the question that the justices have been asked to decide is whether federal trial courts even have the power to consider such challenges, or whether (as the Trump administration argues) those claims are instead barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court, because they are also related to whether one can be deported. The federal courts of appeals have reached conflicting conclusions on the issue, which increases the likelihood that the justices will agree to weigh in.

Suri’s response to the government’s petition for review and the government’s response to Khalil’s petition are both due on Nov. 20. The justices will likely consider both petitions at a private conference sometime early next year.

In June, the Supreme Court granted the federal government’s petition for review in Genalo v. Black, agreeing to address whether there is a point at which a noncitizen has been detained so long that he or she has a constitutional right to a bond hearing and, if so, what standard the government must meet for him or her to remain in detention. That case was scheduled for oral argument in October, but it was dismissed in September because it was moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.

The Trump administration returned to the court later that month, asking the justices to grant a petition for review involving the same questions, which Sauer called “exceptionally important.” The case was filed by a citizen of the Dominican Republic, identified in court filings only as D.C., who has spent most of his adult life in the United States and has three daughters with a U.S. citizen. D.C. was detained on the same day that he finished serving a prison sentence, and the government sought to deport him.

In March 2026, when he had been in immigration custody for almost six-and-a-half months, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer agreed with D.C. that he was entitled to “an individualized bond hearing, with constitutionally adequate procedural safeguards.” The Trump administration is now appealing that decision to the Supreme Court without waiting for a federal appeals court to rule on the case. Sauer told the justices that “granting immediate review would allow the Court to consider” the questions it had already agreed to decide in Black during the 2026-27 term.

D.C.’s response is currently due on Dec. 8; if that deadline remains in place, the court would likely consider the government’s petition sometime in early to mid-January.

In Trump v. Thakur, the justices will consider a petition for review stemming from the 2025 decision to end research grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, National Science Foundation, and National Endowment for the Humanities for researchers at the University of California. The researchers went to federal court, where they argued that the termination of those grants violated (among other things) their rights to free speech and fair treatment, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

A federal district court issued a preliminary order requiring the government to reinstate the grants. The government went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which upheld that decision with regard to the claims on the basis that the administration had ended the grants because of the recipients’ “perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints.”

The court of appeals rejected the government’s contention that it could terminate funding for programs that, in its view, are not in the public interest. “This overlooks that there is a critical distinction between creating or ceasing a particular program (or subsidy, or forum), on one hand, and discriminating against disfavored speaker viewpoints within a program (or subsidy, or forum), on the other,” the 9th Circuit wrote.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. Sauer told the court that “if left to stand, the Ninth Circuit’s decision will establish precedent forcing taxpayers to waste countless dollars on private projects promoting ideologies that their public stewards reject.”

Last week Sauer asked the Supreme Court to distribute the government’s petition, as well as the researchers’ brief opposing review, on Oct. 28, without waiting the 14 days normally prescribed by the court’s rules. This would allow the justices to consider the case at their Nov. 13 conference.

In United States v. Jackson, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to rule on the legality of Trump’s appointment of an acting U.S. attorney in Nevada. Sauer told the justices that the appointment of Sigal Chattah (as well as others around the country) was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.”

Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi said, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

Three men who had been indicted on felony charges in Nevada after Chattah’s designation as the first assistant U.S. attorney sought to have, at a minimum, Chattah disqualified from appearing in the case as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.” The lower courts agreed that Chattah was not eligible to serve as the acting U.S. attorney, and that she could not play any role in the prosecution of the defendants’ cases.

In a 34-page opinion, Judge Eric Miller of the 9th Circuit wrote that the “text and structure” of the FVRA are “unambiguous: The statute does not permit the executive to fill an existing vacancy by designating a new first assistant.” Instead, he reasoned, the FVRA “provides that a first assistant automatically succeeds to a vacant office” only if the first assistant was first assistant when the principal office became vacant. The automatic-succession rule, he concluded, “does not apply to a first assistant” – like Chattah – “who never served under a validly appointed official.” Moreover, Miller continued, the attorney general cannot achieve the same result “by delegating all of the functions and duties of the U.S. Attorney to someone else.”

In a second petition, United States v. Office of the New York State Attorney General, the Trump administration has appealed a ruling against it by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit in a dispute over the appointment of John Sarcone as the Acting U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York. When Sarcone obtained grand jury subpoenas for information from the New York attorney general’s office relating to its investigations of the National Rifle Association and Trump, the office sought to quash the subpoenas on the ground that Sarcone had not been validly appointed.

A federal district court granted that request, and the 2nd Circuit upheld that decision. Sauer came to the Supreme Court in September, where he told the justices that Jackson was a better case in which to consider the validity of Trump’s appointments because the grand jury that issued the subpoenas in the New York case had been discharged and, as a result, the subpoenas were no longer enforceable. He urged the court to hold the New York case until it acts on Jackson.

The defendants challenging Chattah’s appointment have until Nov. 5 to file their brief opposing review; the response of the N.Y. attorney general’s office is currently due on Nov. 2.

There are several other notable petitions pending.

In May 2025, the Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration’s request to temporarily enforce a ban on transgender servicemembers. In a different case just over one year later, a divided panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of an order by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., barring the Trump administration from expelling several challengers to the policy from the military. (At the same time, that panel lifted the part of the order that would have required the military to admit transgender people who want to join the armed forces.)

In its petition for review in United States v. Talbott, filed in August, the federal government asked the Supreme Court to review and eventually reverse the D.C. Circuit’s decision. Sauer called it “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”

The response from the challengers is currently due on Nov. 2.

In Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether and when a federal court can throw out an agency’s action or rule in its entirety – a concept known as “universal vacatur.”

The question comes to the court in a case that began as a pair of challenges (that were later combined) to rules issued to implement parts of a 2022 law that was intended to protect patients from surprise healthcare bills. A federal district court in Texas ruled for the challengers – the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies – but a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed that decision in part.

The case then went to the full 5th Circuit, which threw out some of the challenged provisions. The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court this month, asking the justices to take up the dispute. It pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA, holding that federal courts do not have the authority to enter so-called universal or nationwide injunctions, which prohibit the government from enforcing a policy anywhere in the country. The same logic underlying that case – the idea that courts “can grant ‘complete relief’ to parties before the court but cannot, as a rule, reach beyond them” – should apply to such regulations, Sauer contended.

The challengers’ response is currently due on Nov. 13, although that deadline may be extended.

Petitions filed by Trump’s personal lawyers

Although the federal government filed all of the petitions discussed above, Trump is also seeking Supreme Court review in three petitions filed by his personal lawyers. The most recent petition is also the one that the justices could consider first: Trump v. Clinton, the president’s bid to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.”

U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed the lawsuit, finding (among other things) that Trump had brought his claims too late, and that many of the statements alleged to have been made by the various defendants were “plainly protected by the First Amendment.” Middlebrooks also sanctioned Trump and his attorney, Alina Habba, ordering them to pay nearly $1 million.

On appeal, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit largely upheld Middlebrooks’ decision and affirmed the sanctions orders. The full 11th Circuit rejected Trump’s request for reconsideration, prompting Trump – represented by Richard Klugh – to come to the Supreme Court on Oct. 9. He asked the justices to weigh in on two questions: whether the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended because of his unique role and responsibilities as president, and whether a court can fine the president and his lawyers for making the “substantial, unresolved argument” that the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended.

Through her longtime attorney, David Kendall, Clinton waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition. The case has been distributed to the justices for consideration at their Nov. 6 conference. The court is extremely unlikely to grant review without first calling for Clinton to file a brief opposing review.

In Trump v. CNN, the president is seeking to reinstate his defamation case against cable news giant CNN. Trump contends that when CNN used the phrase “the Big Lie” to describe his insistence that he had actually won the 2020 election, which had been stolen from him, it was attempting to link him with Adolf Hitler and Nazi propaganda – which, Trump said, was defamation.

A federal judge in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, dismissed Trump’s case. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the 11th Circuit upheld that ruling.

In his petition for review, which was filed in August, Trump contended that “CNN falsely and maliciously portrayed” him “as a knowing liar who fabricated objections to the 2020 election, lacked supporting evidence, and deliberately deceived the American people.”

And in July, Trump filed the second of two petitions arising from lawsuits brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a New York department store. The lawsuit leading to the second petition claimed that in June 2019, Trump had defamed her by calling her a liar – saying, among other things, that Carroll “was trying to sell a new book” and that her accusations were “totally false.” A jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million in January 2024.

The 2nd Circuit upheld the award in 2025, finding “ample evidence that Trump was recklessly indifferent to Carroll’s health and safety” and that “Carroll was subjected to ongoing and prolific harassment as a result of these statements, including a multitude of death threats and other threats of physical injury.” The full court of appeals in April declined to rehear the case.

Represented by a private lawyer, Robert Giuffra, Trump argued in his petition for review that in the wake of the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office, the $83.3 million award cannot be allowed to stand. “The threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next,’” Giuffra wrote.

The federal government filed its own petition backing Trump, in which it (like Trump) urged the Supreme Court to also decide whether the court of appeals should have granted then-Attorney General Bondi’s request to recertify that Trump made his statements as part of his role as president and therefore the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case.

Carroll’s response to both petitions is currently due on Oct. 30.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

Recommended Citation: Amy Howe, Another Trump term?, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 27, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/another-trump-term/
